0.title: Everyone Did What Was Right in His Own Eyes: The Book of Judges
0.overview:
The book of Judges is the bridge between conquest and kingdom, and it is a chronicle of descent. Joshua ends with the people standing on Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim, swearing covenant loyalty to the LORD who had given them the land. Judges opens with that loyalty already crumbling and ends with a Levite dismembering the body of his murdered concubine and shipping the pieces across Israel. Between those two points the nation spirals downward through a relentless cycle of apostasy, oppression, crying out, and deliverance. As R.C. Sproul observed, Judges is the Old Testament's most unflinching exposure of what the human heart will do when it is left to itself. It is not pleasant reading. It was never meant to be.

The governing structure of the book is what scholars call the Deuteronomic cycle, drawn straight out of the warnings of Deuteronomy 28: Israel abandons the LORD and serves the Baals; God hands them over to oppressors; in their misery they cry out; God, moved by compassion, raises up a judge who delivers them; the land has rest; the judge dies; and the people sink back into sin, deeper than before. The cycle is not a circle but a downward spiral. Each turn of the wheel finds Israel further from God, and each deliverer is more flawed than the last, until by Samson the judge is scarcely distinguishable from the people he is meant to save.

This is the book's theological genius. Judges does not merely tell us that Israel needed better leaders; it tells us that Israel needed a different kind of King. The fourfold refrain of the final chapters — 'In those days there was no king in Israel' (17:6; 18:1; 19:1; 21:25) — is the heartbeat of the book. Sinclair Ferguson notes that the refrain is not a wistful plea for a monarchy like David's, for even David and his sons would fail. It is a cry, whether the writer fully knew it or not, for the true King — the Lord Jesus Christ, the Judge who does not die, the Deliverer who does not fail, the King whose reign breaks the cycle forever.

So we read Judges as Christians, watching each rescuer rise and fall. Othniel the ideal, Ehud the unlikely, Deborah the bold, Gideon the doubting, Jephthah the outcast, Samson the wasted — every one of them a flickering, partial shadow of the Savior to come. The judges save Israel from Moab and Midian and Philistia; Jesus saves his people from sin and death and hell. The judges deliver for a generation; Jesus delivers forever. And so the darkness of Judges, honestly faced, becomes the black velvet against which the diamond of the gospel blazes. Do not look away from the horror in these pages. Feel it. For only those who feel the weight of 'everyone did what was right in his own eyes' will fall to their knees in gratitude for the King who does what is right in the eyes of his Father, and gives that righteousness to us.

1.title: The Incomplete Conquest
1.text: <sup>1</sup>After the death of Joshua, the people of Israel inquired of the LORD, "Who shall go up first for us against the Canaanites, to fight against them?"<sup>2</sup>The LORD said, "Judah shall go up; behold, I have given the land into his hand."<sup>3</sup>And Judah said to Simeon his brother, "Come up with me into the territory allotted to me, that we may fight against the Canaanites. And I likewise will go with you into the territory allotted to you." So Simeon went with him.<sup>4</sup>Then Judah went up and the LORD gave the Canaanites and the Perizzites into their hand, and they defeated 10,000 of them at Bezek.<sup>5</sup>They found Adoni-bezek at Bezek and fought against him and defeated the Canaanites and the Perizzites.<sup>6</sup>Adoni-bezek fled, but they pursued him and caught him and cut off his thumbs and his big toes.<sup>7</sup>And Adoni-bezek said, "Seventy kings with their thumbs and their big toes cut off used to pick up scraps under my table. As I have done, so God has repaid me." And they brought him to Jerusalem, and he died there.<sup>8</sup>And the men of Judah fought against Jerusalem and captured it and struck it with the edge of the sword and set the city on fire.<sup>9</sup>And afterward the men of Judah went down to fight against the Canaanites who lived in the hill country, in the Negeb, and in the lowland.<sup>10</sup>And Judah went against the Canaanites who lived in Hebron (now the name of Hebron was formerly Kiriath-arba), and they defeated Sheshai and Ahiman and Talmai.<sup>11</sup>From there they went against the inhabitants of Debir. The name of Debir was formerly Kiriath-sepher.<sup>12</sup>And Caleb said, "He who attacks Kiriath-sepher and captures it, I will give him Achsah my daughter as wife."<sup>13</sup>And Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother, captured it. And he gave him Achsah his daughter as wife.<sup>14</sup>When she came to him, she urged him to ask her father for a field. And she dismounted from her donkey, and Caleb said to her, "What do you want?"<sup>15</sup>She said to him, "Give me a blessing. Since you have given me the land of the Negeb, give me also springs of water." And Caleb gave her the upper springs and the lower springs.<sup>16</sup>And the descendants of the Kenite, Moses' father-in-law, went up with the people of Judah from the city of palms into the wilderness of Judah, which lies in the Negeb near Arad, and they went and settled with the people.<sup>17</sup>And Judah went with Simeon his brother, and they defeated the Canaanites who inhabited Zephath and devoted it to destruction. So the name of the city was called Hormah.<sup>18</sup>Judah also captured Gaza with its territory, and Ashkelon with its territory, and Ekron with its territory.<sup>19</sup>And the LORD was with Judah, and he took possession of the hill country, but he could not drive out the inhabitants of the plain because they had chariots of iron.<sup>20</sup>And Hebron was given to Caleb, as Moses had said. And he drove out from it the three sons of Anak.<sup>21</sup>But the people of Benjamin did not drive out the Jebusites who lived in Jerusalem, so the Jebusites have lived with the people of Benjamin in Jerusalem to this day.<sup>22</sup>The house of Joseph also went up against Bethel, and the LORD was with them.<sup>23</sup>And the house of Joseph scouted out Bethel. (Now the name of the city was formerly Luz.)<sup>24</sup>And the spies saw a man coming out of the city, and they said to him, "Please show us the way into the city, and we will deal kindly with you."<sup>25</sup>And he showed them the way into the city. And they struck the city with the edge of the sword, but they let the man and all his family go.<sup>26</sup>And the man went to the land of the Hittites and built a city and called its name Luz. That is its name to this day.<sup>27</sup>Manasseh did not drive out the inhabitants of Beth-shean and its villages, or Taanach and its villages, or the inhabitants of Dor and its villages, or the inhabitants of Ibleam and its villages, or the inhabitants of Megiddo and its villages, for the Canaanites persisted in dwelling in that land.<sup>28</sup>When Israel grew strong, they put the Canaanites to forced labor, but did not drive them out completely.<sup>29</sup>And Ephraim did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer, so the Canaanites lived in Gezer among them.<sup>30</sup>Zebulun did not drive out the inhabitants of Kitron, or the inhabitants of Nahalol, so the Canaanites lived among them, but became subject to forced labor.<sup>31</sup>Asher did not drive out the inhabitants of Acco, or the inhabitants of Sidon or of Ahlab or of Achzib or of Helbah or of Aphik or of Rehob,<sup>32</sup>so the Asherites lived among the Canaanites, the inhabitants of the land, for they did not drive them out.<sup>33</sup>Naphtali did not drive out the inhabitants of Beth-shemesh, or the inhabitants of Beth-anath, so they lived among the Canaanites, the inhabitants of the land. Nevertheless, the inhabitants of Beth-shemesh and of Beth-anath became subject to forced labor for them.<sup>34</sup>The Amorites pressed the people of Dan back into the hill country, for they did not allow them to come down to the plain.<sup>35</sup>The Amorites persisted in dwelling in Mount Heres, in Aijalon, and in Shaalbim, but the hand of the house of Joseph rested heavily on them, and they became subject to forced labor.<sup>36</sup>And the border of the Amorites ran from the ascent of Akrabbim, from Sela and upward.
1.overview:
The book opens exactly as the last one did — Joshua began after the death of Moses, and Judges begins after the death of Joshua — and for eighteen verses it sounds like a sequel. Israel inquires of the LORD before acting, which is the very thing that went undone at Gibeon. Judah is named and given the land in the perfect tense. The strong tribe invites the weak one along. Giants fall at Hebron, Jerusalem is taken and burned, and a young woman gets off her donkey and asks her father for springs.

Then verse 19 puts two clauses in one sentence that will not agree with each other: the LORD was with Judah, and he could not drive out the inhabitants of the plain because they had chariots of iron. The God who drowned Pharaoh's chariots does not have a problem with iron. What changed was not the odds but the eyes.

From there the chapter is a list, and one phrase tolls through it seven times: did not drive out. Manasseh, Ephraim, Zebulun, Asher, Naphtali — and the reason given in verse 28 is not weakness but profit. When Israel grew strong they put the Canaanites to forced labour instead, which is a business decision made by a nation that had itself been in forced labour within living memory.

Two words change at verse 32 and the ground moves. Everywhere else the Canaanites lived among them; of Asher it says the Asherites lived among the Canaanites. And the chapter ends with Dan pressed back into the hills by the people it was sent to dispossess, and a final verse that maps the Amorites' border. Not one person in this chapter rebels against God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The book opens on a grave and a right instinct: after the death of Joshua, Israel asks the LORD who should go up first (v. 1), and the answer names Judah with the promise attached — I have given the land into his hand (v. 2). Judah invites Simeon along (v. 3), and the campaign goes well: ten thousand at Bezek (v. 4), Adoni-bezek captured and confessing that God has repaid him in his own coin (vv. 5-7), Jerusalem taken and burned (v. 8), the giants of Hebron cut down (vv. 9-10), Othniel winning a town and a wife (vv. 11-15), the Kenites settling among them (v. 16). Then verse 19 turns the chapter over, and verse 21 sounds the note that will not stop.
verseByVerse.theology: The first eighteen verses are the only sustained good news in the book. Israel inquires of God before acting, the strong tribe brings the weak one with it, and the LORD gives the enemy into their hand. It is downhill from verse 19, and it never comes back up.
verseByVerse.examples: Verses 10-15 and 20 are lifted almost word for word out of Joshua — the three sons of Anak, Othniel and Achsah, Caleb receiving Hebron (Josh. 15:14-19; 14:13). Judges begins by re-running Joshua's best material, and then goes somewhere Joshua never went.

verseByVerse.quote: After the death of Joshua, the people of Israel inquired of the LORD, "Who shall go up first for us against the Canaanites, to fight against them?" The LORD said, "Judah shall go up; behold, I have given the land into his hand." And Judah said to Simeon his brother, "Come up with me into the territory allotted to me, that we may fight against the Canaanites. And I likewise will go with you into the territory allotted to you." So Simeon went with him. Then Judah went up and the LORD gave the Canaanites and the Perizzites into their hand, and they defeated 10,000 of them at Bezek.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'After the death of Joshua, the people of Israel inquired of the LORD, "Who shall go up first for us against the Canaanites, to fight against them?"'

The book opens exactly as the last one did. Joshua began after the death of Moses; Judges begins after the death of Joshua. Twice now the story has restarted at a funeral.

The difference is what happens next. When Moses died, God spoke first and named a successor before anybody asked. Here nobody is named. Israel asks the question and gets an answer about a tribe, not a man, and the reader should feel the absence: there is no Joshua to follow Joshua.

What they do is right, and mark it, because it will not happen again like this. They inquired of the LORD — the very thing the leaders failed to do at Gibeon, with the priest and the Urim and Thummim standing available in the camp (Josh. 9:14; Num. 27:21). The book of Judges opens on its highest note.

'The LORD said, "Judah shall go up; behold, I have given the land into his hand."'

The answer names the royal tribe, and it comes with the same perfect tense that ran through Joshua: I have given. Nothing about the arrangement has changed. The land is a gift before it is a campaign.

'And Judah said to Simeon his brother, "Come up with me into the territory allotted to me... And I likewise will go with you into the territory allotted to you." So Simeon went with him.'

Then a small thing that turns out to matter. Judah, the largest tribe, invites Simeon, whose towns were scattered inside Judah's own land and who had no border of his own (Josh. 19:1, 9). The strong tribe does not go alone, and the offer runs both ways: come with me, and I will come with you.

Hold that verse, because it is the high-water mark of Israelite brotherhood in this book. In twenty chapters' time the tribes will be at war with each other and one of them will nearly cease to exist.

verseByVerse.quote: They found Adoni-bezek at Bezek and fought against him and defeated the Canaanites and the Perizzites. Adoni-bezek fled, but they pursued him and caught him and cut off his thumbs and his big toes. And Adoni-bezek said, "Seventy kings with their thumbs and their big toes cut off used to pick up scraps under my table. As I have done, so God has repaid me." And they brought him to Jerusalem, and he died there. And the men of Judah fought against Jerusalem and captured it and struck it with the edge of the sword and set the city on fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'They found Adoni-bezek at Bezek and fought against him and defeated the Canaanites and the Perizzites. Adoni-bezek fled, but they pursued him and caught him and cut off his thumbs and his big toes.'

The mutilation is deliberate and it was a known practice: a man without thumbs cannot grip a sword, and a man without big toes cannot balance or run. He is disabled as a warrior and left alive as an exhibit.

'And Adoni-bezek said, "Seventy kings with their thumbs and their big toes cut off used to pick up scraps under my table. As I have done, so God has repaid me."'

Then the prisoner explains what has happened to him, and his explanation is better theology than most of what Israel will manage in the rest of the book.

Seventy men, each of them a king, crawling under his table for food, and he had done to every one of them exactly what has now been done to him. He does not complain, and he does not call it bad luck. As I have done, so God has repaid me.

A Canaanite tyrant, in the hour of his own humiliation, states the moral law of the universe without being taught it. It is the principle Jesus put in a sentence — with the measure you use it will be measured to you (Matt. 7:2) — and the one Paul made flat and unavoidable: whatever one sows, that will he also reap (Gal. 6:7).

Keep the number seventy. It comes back in chapter 9, where an Israelite named Abimelech will murder his seventy brothers on one stone to make himself king. By then it will be Israel doing what the Canaanite king did, and there will be nobody to explain it as the justice of God.

'And the men of Judah fought against Jerusalem and captured it and struck it with the edge of the sword and set the city on fire.'

Judah takes Jerusalem. The city that Judah could not take in Joshua's day (Josh. 15:63) is captured and burned, and for one verse the unfinished business of the last book is finished.

Then read verse 21 and watch it come undone.

verseByVerse.quote: And afterward the men of Judah went down to fight against the Canaanites who lived in the hill country, in the Negeb, and in the lowland. And Judah went against the Canaanites who lived in Hebron (now the name of Hebron was formerly Kiriath-arba), and they defeated Sheshai and Ahiman and Talmai. From there they went against the inhabitants of Debir. The name of Debir was formerly Kiriath-sepher. And Caleb said, "He who attacks Kiriath-sepher and captures it, I will give him Achsah my daughter as wife." And Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother, captured it. And he gave him Achsah his daughter as wife. When she came to him, she urged him to ask her father for a field. And she dismounted from her donkey, and Caleb said to her, "What do you want?" She said to him, "Give me a blessing. Since you have given me the land of the Negeb, give me also springs of water." And Caleb gave her the upper springs and the lower springs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And Judah went against the Canaanites who lived in Hebron... and they defeated Sheshai and Ahiman and Talmai. From there they went against the inhabitants of Debir... And Caleb said, "He who attacks Kiriath-sepher and captures it, I will give him Achsah my daughter as wife." And Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother, captured it.'

A reader who has just finished Joshua will find this familiar, and it is meant to be. These seven verses are Joshua 15:14-19 told again, almost word for word: the same three giants by name, the same challenge, the same nephew, the same daughter.

Judges opens by replaying Joshua's best material. The giants come down, the young man wins the town, the family holds the ground. For the length of a paragraph the new book sounds exactly like the old one.

Remember Othniel's name. When the nation finally collapses into idolatry two chapters from now, he is the first man God raises up to rescue them (3:9), and and the writer records nothing against him.

'When she came to him, she urged him to ask her father for a field. And she dismounted from her donkey, and Caleb said to her, "What do you want?" She said to him, "Give me a blessing. Since you have given me the land of the Negeb, give me also springs of water." And Caleb gave her the upper springs and the lower springs.'

Achsah gets off her donkey to ask.

She has been given land in the Negeb, which is dry country, and a field down there without water is a technicality rather than a farm. So she asks for the one thing that makes what she already has worth having, and she asks her father to his face.

She is given more than she requested: the upper springs and the lower springs, both.

It is the last unmixed good thing in the chapter, and it is a woman asking a generous man for water. Everything after verse 19 is about people who settled for the dry field.

verseByVerse.quote: And the descendants of the Kenite, Moses' father-in-law, went up with the people of Judah from the city of palms into the wilderness of Judah, which lies in the Negeb near Arad, and they went and settled with the people. And Judah went with Simeon his brother, and they defeated the Canaanites who inhabited Zephath and devoted it to destruction. So the name of the city was called Hormah. Judah also captured Gaza with its territory, and Ashkelon with its territory, and Ekron with its territory. And the LORD was with Judah, and he took possession of the hill country, but he could not drive out the inhabitants of the plain because they had chariots of iron. And Hebron was given to Caleb, as Moses had said. And he drove out from it the three sons of Anak. But the people of Benjamin did not drive out the Jebusites who lived in Jerusalem, so the Jebusites have lived with the people of Benjamin in Jerusalem to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And the descendants of the Kenite, Moses' father-in-law, went up with the people of Judah from the city of palms into the wilderness of Judah... and they went and settled with the people.'

A clan of outsiders attaches itself to Israel and moves in. The Kenites were Midianites, descended from Moses' father-in-law, and they are foreigners with no allotment and no claim.

They are also going to matter. In three chapters' time a Kenite woman called Jael will drive a tent peg through the skull of the enemy commander while every Israelite man in the story is somewhere else. The outsiders who joined at the beginning do the work the insiders will not.

'Judah also captured Gaza with its territory, and Ashkelon with its territory, and Ekron with its territory. And the LORD was with Judah, and he took possession of the hill country, but he could not drive out the inhabitants of the plain because they had chariots of iron.'

Here is the hinge of the chapter, and it is one sentence with two halves that do not agree.

The LORD was with Judah. That is the highest thing this book ever says about anybody, and it is said here.

But he could not drive out the inhabitants of the plain because they had chariots of iron.

Could not. Set the two clauses beside each other and the second one collapses. This is the God who put Pharaoh's chariots at the bottom of the sea, dropped a wall flat at Jericho, threw hail down the pass at Beth-horon and stopped the sun over Gibeon. Iron is not a category he has trouble with.

What has changed is not the odds but the eyes. Judah looked at the plain, saw the equipment, and did the arithmetic without including the only factor that had ever mattered. And three chapters later God will destroy nine hundred iron chariots in a single afternoon, apparently to settle the question (4:13-15).

This is how it goes with most of us. We confess the presence of God in general and then draw a map of the places where we assume he cannot help — the entrenched habit, the marriage that has been like this for years, the diagnosis. We give him the hill country and concede the plain.

'And Hebron was given to Caleb, as Moses had said. And he drove out from it the three sons of Anak. But the people of Benjamin did not drive out the Jebusites who lived in Jerusalem, so the Jebusites have lived with the people of Benjamin in Jerusalem to this day.'

Two verses, deliberately side by side, and they are the whole book in miniature.

Caleb, an old man of the previous generation, drove out the giants. Benjamin, of this generation, did not drive out the Jebusites — from the city Judah had already burned in verse 8. The victory of verse 8 was real and it was not held.

The phrase to this day tells the reader how long it lasted. The Jebusites stayed in Jerusalem for four hundred years, until David took the citadel (2 Sam. 5:6-9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–26 — The Man Who Took the Mercy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The house of Joseph goes up against Bethel, and once more the LORD was with them (v. 22). Their scouts find a man coming out of the city and offer him terms: show us the way in and we will deal kindly with you (vv. 23-24). He does, the city falls, and he and his whole family are let go (v. 25). Then verse 26, which is the point of the story: he went to the land of the Hittites and built a city and called it Luz — the old name of Bethel.
verseByVerse.theology: The episode is written to remind the reader of Rahab, and then to differ from her at every point that matters. She asked for mercy and joined the people who gave it; this man took the mercy and left.
verseByVerse.examples: What he does with his life is the sting. He founds a new town and names it after the one he betrayed — the old pagan name, rebuilt somewhere safer. He was spared, and he used the sparing to start Bethel again out of reach.

verseByVerse.quote: The house of Joseph also went up against Bethel, and the LORD was with them. And the house of Joseph scouted out Bethel. (Now the name of the city was formerly Luz.) And the spies saw a man coming out of the city, and they said to him, "Please show us the way into the city, and we will deal kindly with you." And he showed them the way into the city. And they struck the city with the edge of the sword, but they let the man and all his family go. And the man went to the land of the Hittites and built a city and called its name Luz. That is its name to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'The house of Joseph also went up against Bethel, and the LORD was with them. And the house of Joseph scouted out Bethel. (Now the name of the city was formerly Luz.) And the spies saw a man coming out of the city, and they said to him, "Please show us the way into the city, and we will deal kindly with you."'

The scene is familiar on purpose. Spies, a city, a local who helps them in, and a promise of mercy in exchange — this is Jericho again, and the reader is meant to hear it.

'And he showed them the way into the city. And they struck the city with the edge of the sword, but they let the man and all his family go.'

The bargain is kept exactly. He is spared, his household with him, and he walks out of a burning city alive with everyone he loves.

Up to this point the story is Rahab's, told again.

'And the man went to the land of the Hittites and built a city and called its name Luz. That is its name to this day.'

Then the difference, and it is the whole point.

Rahab asked for mercy and then stayed. She hung the cord, gathered her family, came out of Jericho, lived in Israel to this day, and ended up in the family tree of Jesus. She wanted the God who was doing this.

This man takes the mercy and leaves. He goes north out of reach, founds a new town, and names it Luz — the old name of Bethel, the pagan town he has just betrayed. He rebuilds the thing he escaped from, somewhere safer.

He was rescued and he was not changed. He had no complaint against Israel's God and no interest in him either; he took the exit and used it to start again on his own terms.

There are people who accept a rescue from God's people without ever wanting the God who sent it — grateful, undamaged, and gone. Rahab is in Matthew's genealogy. The man of Luz is a footnote with a town named after a place he did not want to leave.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: From here the chapter becomes a list, and one phrase runs through it like a bell. Manasseh did not drive out six named towns (v. 27); when Israel grew strong they put the Canaanites to forced labour instead (v. 28). Ephraim did not (v. 29). Zebulun did not (v. 30). Asher did not (v. 31) — and verse 32 quietly reverses the formula. Naphtali did not (v. 33). And Dan is not merely failing to drive anyone out: the Amorites press Dan back into the hills and will not let them come down (vv. 34-36).
verseByVerse.theology: Nobody in this list rebels. There is no idol yet, no apostasy, no golden calf. There is only a verb repeated seven times in the negative, and a nation that stopped somewhere short of its orders because the campaign was long and the arrangement was profitable.
verseByVerse.examples: Watch the wording change at verse 32. Everywhere else the Canaanites lived among them — Israel is the host. Of Asher it says the Asherites lived among the Canaanites. The minority has changed sides, and nobody voted on it.

verseByVerse.quote: Manasseh did not drive out the inhabitants of Beth-shean and its villages, or Taanach and its villages, or the inhabitants of Dor and its villages, or the inhabitants of Ibleam and its villages, or the inhabitants of Megiddo and its villages, for the Canaanites persisted in dwelling in that land. When Israel grew strong, they put the Canaanites to forced labor, but did not drive them out completely. And Ephraim did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer, so the Canaanites lived in Gezer among them. Zebulun did not drive out the inhabitants of Kitron, or the inhabitants of Nahalol, so the Canaanites lived among them, but became subject to forced labor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Manasseh did not drive out the inhabitants of Beth-shean and its villages, or Taanach and its villages, or the inhabitants of Dor and its villages, or the inhabitants of Ibleam and its villages, or the inhabitants of Megiddo and its villages, for the Canaanites persisted in dwelling in that land.'

The bell starts to toll, and it will not stop for ten verses.

Six towns are named, and the reason given is almost comic in its honesty: the Canaanites persisted in dwelling in that land. Of course they did. That is what people do about their own houses. The question was never whether Canaan would object.

These are the same six towns Joshua listed as Manasseh's and unconquered (Josh. 17:11-12). Nothing has moved in a generation.

'When Israel grew strong, they put the Canaanites to forced labor, but did not drive them out completely.'

Here is the sentence that explains the whole chapter.

The excuse used to be weakness. Joshua 17 said Manasseh could not, and that was stated as a fact rather than a sin. Then Israel grew strong, and the reason for the failure expired — and at the moment the thing became possible, they found something better to do with it.

Forced labour is not a defeat. It is a business decision. Removing an entrenched population from six fortified towns is expensive; keeping them as a permanent workforce is profitable. The command was quietly replaced by a labour policy and everybody did well.

There is a bitter irony in it that Israel seems not to have noticed. This is a nation that was itself in forced labour within living memory, redeemed out of it by God's own hand, and its first act on getting the upper hand is to impose it on somebody else rather than obey.

'And Ephraim did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer... Zebulun did not drive out the inhabitants of Kitron, or the inhabitants of Nahalol, so the Canaanites lived among them, but became subject to forced labor.'

The formula repeats, tribe by tribe, and each entry is shorter than the last. Ephraim — Joshua's own tribe — leaves Gezer exactly where Joshua's book said it was left (Josh. 16:10).

verseByVerse.quote: Asher did not drive out the inhabitants of Acco, or the inhabitants of Sidon or of Ahlab or of Achzib or of Helbah or of Aphik or of Rehob, so the Asherites lived among the Canaanites, the inhabitants of the land, for they did not drive them out. Naphtali did not drive out the inhabitants of Beth-shemesh, or the inhabitants of Beth-anath, so they lived among the Canaanites, the inhabitants of the land. Nevertheless, the inhabitants of Beth-shemesh and of Beth-anath became subject to forced labor for them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Asher did not drive out the inhabitants of Acco, or the inhabitants of Sidon or of Ahlab or of Achzib or of Helbah or of Aphik or of Rehob, so the Asherites lived among the Canaanites, the inhabitants of the land, for they did not drive them out.'

Read verse 32 twice, because the writer has changed one word and it changes everything.

Everywhere else in this chapter the formula is that the Canaanites lived among them. Israel is the household and the Canaanites are the lodgers; the tribe is still the tribe, still in charge, still the thing that defines the place.

Of Asher it says: the Asherites lived among the Canaanites, the inhabitants of the land.

The sentence has turned round. Asher is now the minority in his own allotment, and the Canaanites are described — without comment — as the inhabitants of the land. That is the phrase the book uses for the people God said to remove, and it is now simply the name for whoever actually lives there.

Nobody in Asher voted for that. There was no assembly, no decision, no day on which the tribe agreed to become a minority. It happened the way it always happens, by not doing something for long enough.

'Naphtali did not drive out the inhabitants of Beth-shemesh, or the inhabitants of Beth-anath, so they lived among the Canaanites.'

The same wording again, one tribe later. Two of the northern tribes have stopped being communities of Israel in Canaan and become Israelites living in Canaanite country.

The names in Naphtali's list say what that costs. Beth-shemesh is the house of the sun; Beth-anath is the house of Anath, the Canaanite war goddess. Naphtali is now living among towns named after other gods, and paying rent in the form of forced labour that runs the other way.

verseByVerse.quote: The Amorites pressed the people of Dan back into the hill country, for they did not allow them to come down to the plain. The Amorites persisted in dwelling in Mount Heres, in Aijalon, and in Shaalbim, but the hand of the house of Joseph rested heavily on them, and they became subject to forced labor. And the border of the Amorites ran from the ascent of Akrabbim, from Sela and upward.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'The Amorites pressed the people of Dan back into the hill country, for they did not allow them to come down to the plain.'

The chapter ends at the bottom.

Every other tribe in the list failed to drive somebody out. Dan is being driven. The Amorites push them back off their own allotment and up into the hills, and hold the line: they did not allow them to come down to the plain.

The conquest is now running backwards. In verse 2 God gave the land into Judah's hand; in verse 34 an Israelite tribe is confined to high ground by the people it was sent to dispossess.

'The Amorites persisted in dwelling in Mount Heres, in Aijalon, and in Shaalbim, but the hand of the house of Joseph rested heavily on them, and they became subject to forced labor. And the border of the Amorites ran from the ascent of Akrabbim, from Sela and upward.'

The last verse of the chapter is a border, and it is the wrong nation's border. The chapter that began with God giving Israel a land ends by mapping out where the Amorites live.

Follow what happens to Dan, because it is where the book's darkest chapters come from. A tribe squeezed off its land will not stay squeezed. In chapter 18 the Danites give up on the allotment entirely, march north with six hundred armed men, steal an idol and a priest on the way, and take a quiet town called Laish that had done nothing to anybody. The apostasy at the end of this book begins with the pressure recorded in this verse.

Look back at what has happened across thirty-six verses. Israel began by asking God a question and receiving a promise. It ends with a tribe in the hills, six towns unconquered, two tribes absorbed into the population, and a border drawn for the enemy.

Nobody rebelled. There is not one idol in this chapter, not one act of defiance, not a single person who says no to God. There is only a war that got long, an arrangement that paid, and a verb repeated seven times in the negative.

That is how it is done. Not by a decision to abandon God, but by a series of small settlements, each of them defensible on the day it was made, until the people who were given a country are living in somebody else's.

1.theology:
Nobody rebelled. There is no idol in this chapter, no defiance, no refusal. There is a war that got long, an arrangement that paid, and a verb repeated seven times in the negative. That is the book's diagnosis of how a covenant nation is lost — not by a decision to abandon God but by a series of settlements, each defensible on the day it was made.

Could not. Verse 19 is the hinge, and its two halves cannot both be true in the sense Judah meant them. Iron chariots had never been an obstacle to the God who sank Pharaoh's in the sea, and three chapters later he destroys nine hundred of them in an afternoon (4:13-15). Confessing God's presence in general while mapping the territories where he is assumed to be no help is not a failure of theology. It is a failure to look at what one already believes.

Profit, not weakness. Joshua 17 said Manasseh could not take the six towns, and stated it as fact rather than sin. Here Israel grew strong and put the Canaanites to forced labour instead (v. 28). The excuse expired and the arrangement stayed, because by then it paid — imposed by a people redeemed out of forced labour within living memory.

Mercy without conversion. The man of Bethel is Rahab's story retold and then reversed. He takes the terms, walks out of a burning city with his whole family, and goes off to build a new town named after the old one. He had no quarrel with Israel's God and no interest in him. Rahab wanted the God who was doing this and ended up in the family of Jesus; the man of Luz took the exit and used it to start again on his own terms.
1.examples:
Then: A generation that began by asking God a question ended by keeping the enemy as a workforce, and within a chapter one tribe was living as a minority in its own allotment and another had been pushed off its land altogether. There was no moment at which anybody chose it.

Now: The phrase to test yourself against is not I will not but I could not. Name the plain you have conceded — the habit, the relationship, the fear you have quietly filed under permanent — and ask what changed the day you filed it. It is unlikely to have been new evidence about God. And ask the second question too: what have you kept because it is useful, that God told you to end?

2.title: The Pattern Established
2.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the angel of the LORD went up from Gilgal to Bochim. And he said, "I brought you up from Egypt and brought you into the land that I swore to give to your fathers. I said, 'I will never break my covenant with you,<sup>2</sup>and you shall make no covenant with the inhabitants of this land; you shall break down their altars.' But you have not obeyed my voice. What is this you have done?<sup>3</sup>So now I say, I will not drive them out before you, but they shall become thorns in your sides, and their gods shall be a snare to you."<sup>4</sup>As soon as the angel of the LORD spoke these words to all the people of Israel, the people lifted up their voices and wept.<sup>5</sup>And they called the name of that place Bochim. And they sacrificed there to the LORD.<sup>6</sup>When Joshua dismissed the people, the people of Israel went each to his inheritance to take possession of the land.<sup>7</sup>And the people served the LORD all the days of Joshua, and all the days of the elders who outlived Joshua, who had seen all the great work that the LORD had done for Israel.<sup>8</sup>And Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of the LORD, died at the age of 110 years.<sup>9</sup>And they buried him within the boundaries of his inheritance in Timnath-heres, in the hill country of Ephraim, north of the mountain of Gaash.<sup>10</sup>And all that generation also were gathered to their fathers. And there arose another generation after them who did not know the LORD or the work that he had done for Israel.<sup>11</sup>And the people of Israel did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and served the Baals.<sup>12</sup>And they abandoned the LORD, the God of their fathers, who had brought them out of the land of Egypt. They went after other gods, from among the gods of the peoples who were around them, and bowed down to them. And they provoked the LORD to anger.<sup>13</sup>They abandoned the LORD and served the Baals and the Ashtaroth.<sup>14</sup>So the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he gave them over to plunderers, who plundered them. And he sold them into the hand of their surrounding enemies, so that they could no longer withstand their enemies.<sup>15</sup>Whenever they marched out, the hand of the LORD was against them for harm, as the LORD had warned, and as the LORD had sworn to them. And they were in terrible distress.<sup>16</sup>Then the LORD raised up judges, who saved them out of the hand of those who plundered them.<sup>17</sup>Yet they did not listen to their judges, for they whored after other gods and bowed down to them. They soon turned aside from the way in which their fathers had walked, who had obeyed the commandments of the LORD, and they did not do so.<sup>18</sup>Whenever the LORD raised up judges for them, the LORD was with the judge, and he saved them from the hand of their enemies all the days of the judge. For the LORD was moved to pity by their groaning because of those who afflicted and oppressed them.<sup>19</sup>But whenever the judge died, they turned back and were more corrupt than their fathers, going after other gods, serving them and bowing down to them. They did not drop any of their practices or their stubborn ways.<sup>20</sup>So the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he said, "Because this people have transgressed my covenant that I commanded their fathers and have not obeyed my voice,<sup>21</sup>I will no longer drive out before them any of the nations that Joshua left when he died,<sup>22</sup>in order to test Israel by them, whether they will take care to walk in the way of the LORD as their fathers did, or not."<sup>23</sup>So the LORD left those nations, not driving them out quickly, and he did not give them into the hand of Joshua.
2.overview:
Chapter 1 gave the symptoms; chapter 2 gives the diagnosis and sets out the pattern that will govern everything to the end of the book. It opens with the angel of the LORD coming up from Gilgal — the place of the twelve stones and the first Passover in the land — to a place that is about to be renamed Weepers, and delivering what reads like a legal case: the recital of a covenant perfectly kept, the terms Israel was given, and a six-word charge. But you have not obeyed my voice. Then the oldest question in Scripture, the one asked of a woman standing by a tree: what is this you have done? (Gen. 3:13).

The sentence is not an added penalty but a withdrawal. They would not drive the Canaanites out; now neither will he. The people weep, name the place after the weeping, and sacrifice — and nothing changes. Not one altar comes down.

Then the narrative loops back and repeats the last four verses of Joshua almost word for word (Josh. 24:28-31), in order to add the sentence Joshua never wrote: there arose another generation after them who did not know the LORD or the work that he had done for Israel (v. 10). Faithfulness had lasted exactly as long as the eyewitnesses. Everything Joshua built to prevent this — the stones, the children's question, the reading of the whole law — was still standing, and it did not work.

The rest is the cycle stated in formula: evil done, God's anger, a selling into enemy hands, a judge raised up, and relapse the moment he dies — each turn ending lower than the last. At the centre of it stands verse 18, which is why the book is bearable: the LORD was moved to pity by their groaning.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The angel of the LORD goes up from Gilgal to Bochim and delivers what reads like a legal indictment (v. 1). The recital first: I brought you up from Egypt, I brought you into the land, I said I would never break my covenant with you. Then the terms they were given: make no covenant with the inhabitants, break down their altars. Then the charge, in six words — but you have not obeyed my voice — and a question (v. 2). The sentence follows: I will not drive them out, they will be thorns in your sides and their gods a snare to you (v. 3). The people weep, name the place Weepers, and offer sacrifice (vv. 4-5).
verseByVerse.theology: The sentence is not an added punishment but a withdrawal. God simply stops doing the thing Israel had already stopped wanting done. They would not drive the Canaanites out; now neither will he.
verseByVerse.examples: The question at the end of verse 2 is the oldest question in Scripture. What is this you have done? is what God said to the woman in the garden (Gen. 3:13), and what Pharaoh said to Abraham about Sarah (Gen. 12:18). It is the question asked when the thing is already done and cannot be undone.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the angel of the LORD went up from Gilgal to Bochim. And he said, "I brought you up from Egypt and brought you into the land that I swore to give to your fathers. I said, 'I will never break my covenant with you, and you shall make no covenant with the inhabitants of this land; you shall break down their altars.' But you have not obeyed my voice. What is this you have done? So now I say, I will not drive them out before you, but they shall become thorns in your sides, and their gods shall be a snare to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now the angel of the LORD went up from Gilgal to Bochim. And he said, "I brought you up from Egypt and brought you into the land that I swore to give to your fathers. I said, 'I will never break my covenant with you.'"'

Two things about the speaker before anything else. He is called the angel of the LORD, and he speaks as God in the first person — I brought you up from Egypt — without any of the usual thus says the LORD. Whatever else is going on here, this figure does not report God's words. He uses them as his own.

He comes up from Gilgal. That is not scene-setting. Gilgal is where the twelve stones out of the Jordan were set up, where the whole nation was circumcised, where the reproach of Egypt was rolled away and the first Passover in the land was eaten. The messenger travels from the place where the covenant was celebrated to a place that is about to be renamed Weepers.

What follows is built like a legal case, and the order matters. First the recital of what God has done and promised, all of it kept: brought you up, brought you in, and I will never break my covenant with you. There is no complaint on that side of the ledger.

'"and you shall make no covenant with the inhabitants of this land; you shall break down their altars.' But you have not obeyed my voice. What is this you have done?"'

Then the terms, then the charge. Two commands had been given, one negative and one positive: make no treaties, and pull down the altars. Israel had done neither. Chapter 1 is the evidence, and the charge is six words long.

Then a question, which is the oldest question in the Bible. What is this you have done? God asked it of a woman standing beside a tree with the fruit already eaten (Gen. 3:13). It is not a request for information. It is what is said when the thing is finished and cannot be taken back.

'"So now I say, I will not drive them out before you, but they shall become thorns in your sides, and their gods shall be a snare to you."'

The sentence is not an extra penalty added on. It is a withdrawal. God stops doing the thing Israel had already stopped wanting done.

They would not drive the Canaanites out. Very well: neither will he. And the two consequences he names are exactly what Moses had warned forty years earlier, almost word for word — thorns in your sides, and a snare (Num. 33:55). What was a warning is now a verdict.

See which of the two is the deadlier. Thorns wound; a snare catches. The Canaanites will be an irritation, and their gods will be a trap — and the whole rest of this book is Israel walking into it.

There is a kind of judgment that consists in being allowed to keep what you insisted on having. Paul describes it three times in one chapter with a single phrase: God gave them up (Rom. 1:24, 26, 28). It is the most frightening thing in this passage, and it did not require God to do anything at all.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as the angel of the LORD spoke these words to all the people of Israel, the people lifted up their voices and wept. And they called the name of that place Bochim. And they sacrificed there to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'As soon as the angel of the LORD spoke these words to all the people of Israel, the people lifted up their voices and wept. And they called the name of that place Bochim. And they sacrificed there to the LORD.'

The response looks right. They weep, they name the place after the weeping, and they offer sacrifice. A congregation in tears and an altar smoking — on any ordinary reckoning this is a revival meeting.

Nothing changes. Not one Canaanite is driven out the next morning. Not one altar comes down. The place is given a name that commemorates the emotion, and within a few verses the same people are bowing to Baal.

That is the reason this scene is in the book. It is a warning about a particular kind of religious experience: real feeling, genuine tears, an actual sacrifice, and no change of direction whatever.

Paul makes the distinction exactly. Godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death (2 Cor. 7:10). The difference is not in the intensity of the sorrow but in what happens afterwards, and it is often not visible on the day.

Weeping at what a sin has cost is not the same as hating the sin. Israel had just been told about thorns and snares; they wept at the sentence. It is possible to leave a church service genuinely moved, having felt something true, and to have moved nothing.

The name stuck, and it is the right name. This place is not called Repentance. It is called Weepers.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–10 — A Generation That Did Not Know
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The narrative goes back to fill in what happened after Joshua dismissed the people (v. 6). Israel served the LORD all the days of Joshua, and all the days of the elders who outlived him and had seen all the great work that the LORD had done (v. 7). Joshua dies at a hundred and ten and is buried in his own inheritance (vv. 8-9). And then verse 10, which is the sentence the whole book turns on: that generation was gathered to its fathers, and there arose another generation after them who did not know the LORD or the work that he had done for Israel.
verseByVerse.theology: These verses are Joshua 24:28-31 told a second time, almost word for word. Judges repeats the end of the previous book in order to add the one line Joshua never wrote — what happened next.
verseByVerse.examples: Two things are not known, and the second explains the first. They did not know the work, and so they did not know the LORD. The generation that could remember the river opening had died, and what had not been handed on was not a doctrine but an eyewitness account.

verseByVerse.quote: When Joshua dismissed the people, the people of Israel went each to his inheritance to take possession of the land. And the people served the LORD all the days of Joshua, and all the days of the elders who outlived Joshua, who had seen all the great work that the LORD had done for Israel. And Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of the LORD, died at the age of 110 years. And they buried him within the boundaries of his inheritance in Timnath-heres, in the hill country of Ephraim, north of the mountain of Gaash.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'When Joshua dismissed the people, the people of Israel went each to his inheritance to take possession of the land. And the people served the LORD all the days of Joshua, and all the days of the elders who outlived Joshua, who had seen all the great work that the LORD had done for Israel.'

The narrative jumps backwards. Joshua is alive again, dismissing the assembly at Shechem, and the reader is being taken round the same corner a second time.

These four verses are the last four verses of the book of Joshua, repeated almost word for word (Josh. 24:28-31). The writer is not padding. He is quoting the end of the previous book so that he can add one sentence to it that Joshua never wrote.

Before that, look closely at the clause that describes the faithful generation, because it contains the whole problem. They served the LORD all the days of Joshua and of the elders who had seen all the great work that the LORD had done for Israel.

Faithfulness lasted exactly as long as the eyewitnesses lasted. Not as long as the teaching, or the institutions, or the stones at Gilgal — as long as the men who had personally watched the river stop.

'And Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of the LORD, died at the age of 110 years. And they buried him within the boundaries of his inheritance in Timnath-heres.'

He is buried, with the title he was given only at his death, in the town he asked for after everyone else had been housed and then had to rebuild himself.

The generation that opened this chapter weeping at Bochim is the generation that buried him.

verseByVerse.quote: And all that generation also were gathered to their fathers. And there arose another generation after them who did not know the LORD or the work that he had done for Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And all that generation also were gathered to their fathers. And there arose another generation after them who did not know the LORD or the work that he had done for Israel.'

This is the verse the book turns on, and everything that follows for twenty chapters is commentary on it.

Take the two halves of what they did not know, because the order is the explanation. They did not know the work that he had done for Israel, and they did not know the LORD. The second follows from the first.

These were not pagans. They were the children and grandchildren of the men who crossed the Jordan. They lived in the land, ate its produce, and knew the name of their national God. What they had not been given was the account — the river standing in a heap at a town called Adam, the wall going down flat, the hail in the pass at Beth-horon, the day that would not end. They had the country and not the story.

Ask how that happened in one generation, because everything in Joshua was built to prevent it. Twelve stones were carried out of the riverbed and set up at Gilgal for the express purpose of provoking a child's question — when your children ask in time to come, What do those stones mean? (Josh. 4:6, 21). The whole law was read aloud in a valley with the women, the little ones and the foreigners standing there. A stone was set up at Shechem because it had heard.

All of that machinery existed, and it did not work. Somewhere between the funeral of the last eyewitness and the next harvest, the answering stopped.

The stones did not fail; the stones were still standing. What failed was that somebody's father, walking past them for the fortieth time, did not say anything.

See, too, what is not said here. It does not say the next generation rejected the LORD, or argued with him, or chose other gods in preference. It says they did not know him. There was no controversy. There was an absence, and the Baals moved into it.

The church has never been more than one silence away from this. Faith is not carried in the blood and it does not transmit by proximity to the building. It arrives, always, by somebody telling somebody, and it stops when they stop.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–15 — The Baals, and the Selling
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first two turns of the cycle are stated in formula. Israel did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and served the Baals (v. 11); they abandoned the LORD who brought them out of Egypt and went after the gods of the peoples around them (vv. 12-13). So the anger of the LORD was kindled, and he gave them over to plunderers and sold them into the hand of their enemies (v. 14). Whenever they went out, the hand of the LORD was against them for harm, exactly as he had warned, and they were in terrible distress (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: Baal was the storm god who was supposed to control the rain, and Israel had just moved into farming country. The apostasy of this book does not begin in philosophy; it begins in agriculture, with new settlers taking local advice about how to get a harvest.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 14 will not let God be absent from the disaster. He gave them over; he sold them, as a master sells a slave. Israel's defeats in this book are not the failure of their God to protect them. They are his discipline, and he says so before it starts.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and served the Baals. And they abandoned the LORD, the God of their fathers, who had brought them out of the land of Egypt. They went after other gods, from among the gods of the peoples who were around them, and bowed down to them. And they provoked the LORD to anger. They abandoned the LORD and served the Baals and the Ashtaroth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And the people of Israel did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and served the Baals.'

The formula that will run through the rest of the book is used for the first time here, and it will appear seven more times before the end. Everything in Judges is measured by that phrase — in the sight of the LORD. Not by what worked, or what the neighbours thought.

Now consider what serving the Baals actually looked like on the ground, because it was not a philosophical decision. Baal was the storm god. He was believed to control the rain, and therefore the barley, and therefore whether a family ate in the spring.

Israel had just moved out of forty years of manna and into a farming economy, in a country they did not understand, and the locals had a settled body of expertise about how to get a harvest out of this particular soil. The Baals came with the agricultural advice.

That is how the apostasy of Judges begins. Not with a decision to abandon the God of the exodus, but with new settlers taking sensible local counsel about rainfall.

'And they abandoned the LORD, the God of their fathers, who had brought them out of the land of Egypt. They went after other gods, from among the gods of the peoples who were around them, and bowed down to them. And they provoked the LORD to anger. They abandoned the LORD and served the Baals and the Ashtaroth.'

The narrator refuses the sensible description and uses the accurate one. Twice in three verses: they abandoned the LORD.

He attaches the identifying clause every time: the God of their fathers, who had brought them out of the land of Egypt. That is the whole indictment in a relative clause. They exchanged the God who had actually done something for them — verifiably, within family memory — for gods who were credited with the weather.

Jeremiah puts the same trade in a picture that has never been improved on: my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, and hewed out cisterns for themselves, broken cisterns that can hold no water (Jer. 2:13).

verseByVerse.quote: So the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he gave them over to plunderers, who plundered them. And he sold them into the hand of their surrounding enemies, so that they could no longer withstand their enemies. Whenever they marched out, the hand of the LORD was against them for harm, as the LORD had warned, and as the LORD had sworn to them. And they were in terrible distress.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'So the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he gave them over to plunderers, who plundered them. And he sold them into the hand of their surrounding enemies, so that they could no longer withstand their enemies.'

The second turn of the cycle, and the writer will not let God stand at a distance from it.

Read the verbs. God gave them over. God sold them. The raiders who came across the border every harvest were not a geopolitical accident, and Israel's collapse in the field was not the failure of their God to turn up. He is named as the agent.

Sold is the harder of the two words. It is what a man does with a slave he no longer wants under his roof, and it is used deliberately of a nation God had bought out of slavery himself.

'Whenever they marched out, the hand of the LORD was against them for harm, as the LORD had warned, and as the LORD had sworn to them. And they were in terrible distress.'

Then the clause that keeps this from being cruelty: as the LORD had warned. None of this is a surprise. Deuteronomy had set it out in advance, in detail, in public, and read it aloud to the whole nation between two mountains with the children present (Deut. 28:25).

What is happening to Israel is precisely what they were told would happen, by the God they were told it by, and they had heard it read.

Then the last four words, which are not a verdict but an observation: they were in terrible distress. The narrator does not gloat. He has just explained that the misery is deserved, announced and self-inflicted, and he still records that it was terrible.

That matters for what comes three verses later, because the God who sold them is about to be described as unable to bear the noise they make.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Then the turn that keeps the book going: the LORD raised up judges, who saved them out of the hand of those who plundered them (v. 16). And immediately the qualification — they did not listen even to the judges, but whored after other gods and turned aside quickly (v. 17). Verse 18 gives the reason any of it happens at all: the LORD was with the judge, and he was moved to pity by their groaning. And verse 19 closes the loop: whenever the judge died they turned back and were more corrupt than their fathers, and dropped none of their practices or their stubborn ways.
verseByVerse.theology: The word for what the judges did is yasha, to save — the root behind the names Joshua and Jesus. Every judge in this book is a small, temporary, mortal salvation, and the writer says exactly what is wrong with every one of them in verse 19: they die.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 18 is the tenderest sentence in the book and the reason the cycle does not simply end. God is not moved by their repentance, which is not mentioned, nor by their prayers, which are not recorded here. He is moved by their groaning — the noise people make under a weight they chose to pick up.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD raised up judges, who saved them out of the hand of those who plundered them. Yet they did not listen to their judges, for they whored after other gods and bowed down to them. They soon turned aside from the way in which their fathers had walked, who had obeyed the commandments of the LORD, and they did not do so.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then the LORD raised up judges, who saved them out of the hand of those who plundered them.'

One word turns the chapter: then. There is nothing before it to explain it. Israel has not repented, has not asked, has not changed. The previous verse ended in distress and this one begins with rescue, and the only thing between them is God.

Look at who does what. The LORD raised up; the judges saved. Israel is the object of both verbs and the subject of neither.

The word for what the judges do is yasha, to save or deliver, and it is the root behind two names. Joshua is Yehoshua, the LORD saves. So is Jesus, and Matthew explains the name when it is given: you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins (Matt. 1:21).

Every judge in this book is a small, borrowed, temporary version of that, raised up for one crisis in one region and then buried.

'Yet they did not listen to their judges, for they whored after other gods and bowed down to them. They soon turned aside from the way in which their fathers had walked.'

The word the narrator chooses for the idolatry is deliberately offensive, and he will use it again. They whored after other gods. It is the vocabulary of a betrayed marriage, and it is the settled biblical way of describing what idolatry actually is — not an intellectual error but adultery against someone who has a claim.

The timing in that verse is the worst part. They did not listen to their judges — which means this was happening while the rescue was going on. Not after the danger passed and gratitude cooled. During.

verseByVerse.quote: Whenever the LORD raised up judges for them, the LORD was with the judge, and he saved them from the hand of their enemies all the days of the judge. For the LORD was moved to pity by their groaning because of those who afflicted and oppressed them. But whenever the judge died, they turned back and were more corrupt than their fathers, going after other gods, serving them and bowing down to them. They did not drop any of their practices or their stubborn ways.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Whenever the LORD raised up judges for them, the LORD was with the judge, and he saved them from the hand of their enemies all the days of the judge. For the LORD was moved to pity by their groaning because of those who afflicted and oppressed them.'

Here is the sentence that keeps this book from being unbearable.

The secret of every deliverance is given first, and it is the same phrase that explained Judah's victory in chapter 1: the LORD was with the judge. Never the man's ability. The book will make that unmistakable by choosing the least likely men it can find.

Then the reason God does it at all, and it is not what a reader expects after seven verses of apostasy. Not because they repented; no repentance is mentioned. Not because they prayed; no prayer is recorded here. The LORD was moved to pity by their groaning.

Groaning is not repentance. It is the noise a person makes under a weight, and this particular weight was picked up voluntarily and warned about in advance. God is moved by the sound of people suffering the exact consequences he told them would come.

The verb behind moved to pity describes something turning over inside — the physical sensation of being unable to watch. It is the same movement recorded when God heard a different groaning from a different slavery: God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant (Ex. 2:24).

'But whenever the judge died, they turned back and were more corrupt than their fathers, going after other gods, serving them and bowing down to them. They did not drop any of their practices or their stubborn ways.'

The loop closes. Two words in that verse tell you what kind of shape this book has.

The first is died. The trigger for every relapse is a funeral. The deliverance lasted exactly as long as the deliverer, every time, without exception, for the whole book.

The second is more. They were more corrupt than their fathers. This is not a circle that returns to where it started; each turn ends lower than the last. By the final chapters, Israelites will be doing to each other what the Canaanite king did to seventy kings in chapter 1.

Put the two together and the diagnosis is structural rather than moral. The system does not fail because the judges were bad; several of them were remarkable. It fails because they were mortal, and because the people were not changed by being rescued.

The letter to the Hebrews puts the finger on exactly this weakness in the old arrangement: the former priests were many in number, because they were prevented by death from continuing in office — but he holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues for ever (Heb. 7:23-24).

Israel did not need a better judge. Every improvement on Othniel would still be buried. What was needed was a deliverer against whom the trigger of verse 19 could not be pulled, and the only qualification that mattered was that he should not stay dead.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter ends with God stating a purpose behind the unfinished conquest. Because this people have transgressed the covenant and not obeyed (v. 20), he will no longer drive out any of the nations Joshua left when he died (v. 21) — in order to test Israel by them, whether they will take care to walk in the way of the LORD as their fathers did, or not (v. 22). So the nations were left, not driven out quickly (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: The same nations are two things at once. In verse 3 they are the consequence of Israel's disobedience; in verse 22 they are the instrument of God's testing. Scripture holds both without any sense of strain, and a reader who insists on choosing one will misread the rest of the book.
verseByVerse.examples: The last clause of verse 23 is quietly devastating: he did not give them into the hand of Joshua. Even the best generation in the story did not receive everything. The unfinished business was already unfinished before anybody now living was born.

verseByVerse.quote: So the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he said, "Because this people have transgressed my covenant that I commanded their fathers and have not obeyed my voice, I will no longer drive out before them any of the nations that Joshua left when he died, in order to test Israel by them, whether they will take care to walk in the way of the LORD as their fathers did, or not." So the LORD left those nations, not driving them out quickly, and he did not give them into the hand of Joshua.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'So the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he said, "Because this people have transgressed my covenant that I commanded their fathers and have not obeyed my voice, I will no longer drive out before them any of the nations that Joshua left when he died."'

The decision of verse 3 is restated as settled policy. The nations stay.

'"in order to test Israel by them, whether they will take care to walk in the way of the LORD as their fathers did, or not."'

Then a purpose clause that changes how the whole book must be read.

The same Canaanites are two things at once. In verse 3 they are the consequence of Israel's disobedience — thorns and a snare, the natural result of a job left unfinished. In verse 22 they are an instrument in God's hand, deliberately left in place in order to test.

Scripture puts those two sentences nineteen verses apart and shows no anxiety about it. The thing Israel brought on itself is the thing God is using. A reader who insists on choosing one of those and dropping the other will misread everything that follows, and will also misread most of his own life.

What is being tested is not their theology but their walking: whether they will take care to walk in the way of the LORD as their fathers did. The exam is conducted over a lifetime and marked by ordinary behaviour.

'So the LORD left those nations, not driving them out quickly, and he did not give them into the hand of Joshua.'

The last clause of the chapter is easy to walk past and should not be: he did not give them into the hand of Joshua.

Even the best generation in this history did not get everything. The man who left nothing undone of all that the LORD commanded Moses (Josh. 11:15) still died with nations standing in the land, and the writer says plainly that this was God's doing and not Joshua's failure.

That is a strange comfort, and it is a real one. There was never a moment in Israel's story when the work was finished and the ground entirely held. There is not one in ours either. The Canaanite left standing in a believer's life is not always evidence of a battle lost; sometimes it is the examination room, left standing on purpose, by a God who has already announced both that he is angry and that he intends to see how they walk.

2.theology:
Judgment as withdrawal. God's sentence at Bochim is to stop doing what Israel had already stopped wanting done: I will not drive them out before you (v. 3). The thorns and the snare are the exact words Moses had used as a warning forty years earlier (Num. 33:55), and the most frightening thing about the judgment is that it required God to do nothing at all. Paul names the same act three times in one chapter — God gave them up (Rom. 1:24, 26, 28).

One generation. Verse 10 does not say the next generation rejected God or chose other gods in preference. It says they did not know him, and it puts the two ignorances in order: they did not know the work, and so they did not know the LORD. They had the country and not the story. Faith is not carried in the blood and does not transmit by proximity to a building; it arrives by somebody telling somebody, and it stops when they stop.

Moved by groaning, not by repentance. Verse 18 gives the reason God keeps raising up deliverers, and it is not Israel's contrition, which is not mentioned, nor their prayers, which are not recorded. He was moved to pity by their groaning — the noise people make under a weight they picked up themselves after being warned. It is the same movement as Exodus 2:24, and it is the only reason this book has more than three chapters.

The flaw is mortality. The trigger for every relapse is stated twice and it is a funeral: whenever the judge died, they turned back (v. 19). The system fails not because the judges were poor — several were remarkable — but because they were buried, and because being rescued did not change anybody. Hebrews puts its finger on the identical weakness in the old priesthood: they were many because they were prevented by death from continuing in office, but he continues for ever (Heb. 7:23-24). Israel did not need a better judge. It needed one who would not stay dead.
2.examples:
Then: A nation wept at a place they named after the weeping, offered sacrifices, and drove out nobody. A generation later their children knew the name of their God and nothing he had done, and started taking farming advice from the neighbours about which god sent rain.

Now: Two tests come out of this chapter. The first is Bochim: genuine tears, a real sacrifice, and no Canaanite driven out by Tuesday. Ask what actually changed after the last time you were deeply moved. The second is verse 10, and it is aimed at parents and churches rather than at individuals. The stones at Gilgal were still standing when that generation grew up. What had stopped was somebody answering the question.

3.title: Othniel, Ehud, and Shamgar
3.text: <sup>1</sup>Now these are the nations that the LORD left, to test Israel by them, that is, all in Israel who had not experienced all the wars in Canaan.<sup>2</sup>It was only in order that the generations of the people of Israel might know war, to teach war to those who had not known it before.<sup>3</sup>These are the nations: the five lords of the Philistines and all the Canaanites and the Sidonians and the Hivites who lived on Mount Lebanon, from Mount Baal-hermon as far as Lebo-hamath.<sup>4</sup>They were for the testing of Israel, to know whether Israel would obey the commandments of the LORD, which he commanded their fathers by the hand of Moses.<sup>5</sup>So the people of Israel lived among the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites.<sup>6</sup>And their daughters they took to themselves for wives, and their own daughters they gave to their sons, and they served their gods.<sup>7</sup>And the people of Israel did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. They forgot the LORD their God and served the Baals and the Asheroth.<sup>8</sup>Therefore the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he sold them into the hand of Cushan-rishathaim king of Mesopotamia. And the people of Israel served Cushan-rishathaim eight years.<sup>9</sup>But when the people of Israel cried out to the LORD, the LORD raised up a deliverer for the people of Israel, who saved them, Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother.<sup>10</sup>The Spirit of the LORD was upon him, and he judged Israel. He went out to war, and the LORD gave Cushan-rishathaim king of Mesopotamia into his hand. And his hand prevailed over Cushan-rishathaim.<sup>11</sup>So the land had rest for forty years. Then Othniel the son of Kenaz died.<sup>12</sup>And the people of Israel again did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, and the LORD strengthened Eglon the king of Moab against Israel, because they had done what was evil in the sight of the LORD.<sup>13</sup>He gathered to himself the Ammonites and the Amalekites, and went and defeated Israel. And they took possession of the city of palms.<sup>14</sup>And the people of Israel served Eglon the king of Moab eighteen years.<sup>15</sup>Then the people of Israel cried out to the LORD, and the LORD raised up for them a deliverer, Ehud, the son of Gera, the Benjaminite, a left-handed man. The people of Israel sent tribute by him to Eglon the king of Moab.<sup>16</sup>And Ehud made for himself a sword with two edges, a cubit in length, and he bound it on his right thigh under his clothes.<sup>17</sup>And he presented the tribute to Eglon king of Moab. Now Eglon was a very fat man.<sup>18</sup>And when Ehud had finished presenting the tribute, he sent away the people who carried the tribute.<sup>19</sup>But he himself turned back at the idols near Gilgal and said, "I have a secret message for you, O king." And he commanded, "Silence." And all his attendants went out from his presence.<sup>20</sup>And Ehud came to him as he was sitting alone in his cool roof chamber. And Ehud said, "I have a message from God for you." And he arose from his seat.<sup>21</sup>And Ehud reached with his left hand, took the sword from his right thigh, and thrust it into his belly.<sup>22</sup>And the hilt also went in after the blade, and the fat closed over the blade, for he did not pull the sword out of his belly; and the dung came out.<sup>23</sup>Then Ehud went out into the porch and closed the doors of the roof chamber behind him and locked them.<sup>24</sup>When he had gone, the servants came, and when they saw that the doors of the roof chamber were locked, they thought, "Surely he is relieving himself in the closet of the cool chamber."<sup>25</sup>And they waited till they were embarrassed. But when he still did not open the doors of the roof chamber, they took the key and opened them, and there lay their lord dead on the floor.<sup>26</sup>Ehud escaped while they delayed, and he passed beyond the idols and escaped to Seirah.<sup>27</sup>When he arrived, he sounded the trumpet in the hill country of Ephraim. Then the people of Israel went down with him from the hill country, and he was their leader.<sup>28</sup>And he said to them, "Follow after me, for the LORD has given your enemies the Moabites into your hand." So they went down after him and seized the fords of the Jordan against the Moabites and did not allow anyone to pass over.<sup>29</sup>And they killed at that time about 10,000 of the Moabites, all strong, able-bodied men; not a man escaped.<sup>30</sup>So Moab was subdued that day under the hand of Israel. And the land had rest for eighty years.<sup>31</sup>After him was Shamgar the son of Anath, who killed 600 of the Philistines with an oxgoad, and he also saved Israel.
3.overview:
The chapter opens by explaining the unfinished conquest twice over. The nations were left to test Israel — and, stranger, in order that the generations of the people of Israel might know war, to teach war to those who had not known it before (v. 2). This was a generation born after the fighting stopped, living in houses it had not built and vineyards it had not planted, that had never once had to depend on God against anybody. The enemy left standing is called a school.

They fail the test in one verse, and the failure runs in a sequence with no pause in it: they took wives, they gave daughters, and they served their gods (v. 6). Nobody married a Canaanite in order to worship Baal. The worship arrived at the end of a chain that began with a wedding, which is precisely the reason Moses gave for the rule (Deut. 7:4).

Then three deliverers, and no two of them alike. Othniel is the model: Caleb's family, the Spirit of the LORD on him, forty years of rest — and then the word that ends every judge, died.
