verseByVerse.examples: Meroz is cursed for doing nothing, and it is never mentioned again — not in this book, not anywhere in Scripture. There is no territory, no clan, no descendant, no further trace of the place. Everything that survives of Meroz is the sentence in which it is cursed.

verseByVerse.quote: "The kings came, they fought; then fought the kings of Canaan, at Taanach, by the waters of Megiddo; they got no spoils of silver. From heaven the stars fought, from their courses they fought against Sisera. The torrent Kishon swept them away, the ancient torrent, the torrent Kishon. March on, my soul, with might! "Then loud beat the horses' hoofs with the galloping, galloping of his steeds. "Curse Meroz, says the angel of the LORD, curse its inhabitants thoroughly, because they did not come to the help of the LORD, to the help of the LORD against the mighty.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'"The kings came, they fought; then fought the kings of Canaan, at Taanach, by the waters of Megiddo; they got no spoils of silver."'

The last clause is the poem's first blow. These kings came for plunder — that is what the campaign was for — and they went home with nothing, if they went home.

'"From heaven the stars fought, from their courses they fought against Sisera. The torrent Kishon swept them away, the ancient torrent, the torrent Kishon."'

Here is what chapter 4 did not tell us. It said only that the LORD routed Sisera, and left the mechanism out.

The song fills it in with a storm. The heavens dropped water in verse 4; here the Kishon comes down. That river is a trickle for most of the year and a torrent when the rain falls on the hills above it, and the plain of Megiddo turns to a bog in an afternoon.

Nine hundred chariots of iron, on flat ground, in mud. The weight that made them irresistible on a dry plain is what fixed them where they stood, and the army that had terrorised the north for twenty years was destroyed by weather and could not run.

The line above it is bigger still: from heaven the stars fought, from their courses they fought against Sisera. Whatever precisely that means — the storm, the timing, the constellations that governed the seasons in Canaanite religion — the claim is that the created order itself was ranged against him.

Sisera worshipped gods who were supposed to run the weather. The weather killed him.

'"Curse Meroz, says the angel of the LORD, curse its inhabitants thoroughly, because they did not come to the help of the LORD, to the help of the LORD against the mighty."'

Then the harshest sentence in the song, which is not aimed at Canaan at all.

Meroz was an Israelite settlement, evidently near enough to the battle to have come. Reuben was chided and Dan was asked a question; Meroz is cursed, and thoroughly, and the curse is pronounced by the angel of the LORD — the same figure who stood at Bochim in chapter 2 and delivered the covenant lawsuit.

The charge is not that Meroz fought on the wrong side. It is that they did not come.

Mark the phrasing, repeated for emphasis: not to the help of Israel, or of Barak, or of Deborah, but to the help of the LORD against the mighty. God is spoken of as though he needed reinforcements, which he plainly did not, and the men of Meroz are held responsible for not turning up to a battle he had already won.

Here is the strangest thing about Meroz. It is never mentioned again. Not in this book, not in the rest of the Old Testament, not anywhere. There is no territory, no clan, no genealogy, no ruin identified with certainty. A whole community's entire trace in Scripture is one line cursing it for staying home.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jael is blessed in the strongest terms the language has — most blessed of women, of tent-dwelling women most blessed (v. 24) — and the deed is told again, slowly: the milk in a noble's bowl, the hand to the peg and the right hand to the workmen's mallet, the shattered temple, and the hammering repetition of him sinking and falling and lying still (vv. 25-27). Then the song moves to a window in Canaan, where another woman is waiting for the same man. Sisera's mother peers through the lattice and asks why his chariot is so long in coming, and her ladies answer, and she answers herself (vv. 28-30).
verseByVerse.theology: The song sets two women side by side and lets the reader look at both. One kills the commander with a tool she uses every day. The other is at a window, working out an explanation for why he is late, and there is nothing in the poem to stop the reader pitying her.
verseByVerse.examples: What she comforts herself with is the worst line in the song: they are delayed because the men are dividing the spoil, a womb or two for every man. That is a mother reassuring herself that her son is late because his soldiers are raping captured women. The song does not soften what the army in the valley actually was.

verseByVerse.quote: "Most blessed of women be Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, of tent-dwelling women most blessed. He asked for water and she gave him milk; she brought him curds in a noble's bowl. She sent her hand to the tent peg and her right hand to the workmen's mallet; she struck Sisera; she crushed his head; she shattered and pierced his temple. Between her feet he sank, he fell, he lay still; between her feet he sank, he fell; where he sank, there he fell—dead. "Out of the window she peered, the mother of Sisera wailed through the lattice: 'Why is his chariot so long in coming? Why tarry the hoofbeats of his chariots?' Her wisest princesses answer, indeed, she answers herself, 'Have they not found and divided the spoil?— A womb or two for every man; spoil of dyed materials for Sisera, spoil of dyed materials embroidered, two pieces of dyed work embroidered for the neck as spoil?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
'"Most blessed of women be Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, of tent-dwelling women most blessed."'

The song answers the curse of Meroz with a blessing, and it is put in the strongest form Hebrew has.

There is only one other person in Scripture greeted in these words. When Mary comes to Elizabeth's house, Elizabeth cries out, blessed are you among women (Luke 1:42). The two people so described are the mother of the Lord and a Kenite housewife with a mallet, and both blessings are spoken by a woman about a woman, in a house, about something God has done that nobody expected.

'"He asked for water and she gave him milk; she brought him curds in a noble's bowl. She sent her hand to the tent peg and her right hand to the workmen's mallet; she struck Sisera; she crushed his head; she shattered and pierced his temple."'

The poem tells the deed more slowly than the prose did, and it names the tools twice: the tent peg, and the workmen's mallet. Not a weapon that happened to be lying about — the equipment of a trade, in the hand that used it professionally.

'"Between her feet he sank, he fell, he lay still; between her feet he sank, he fell; where he sank, there he fell — dead."'

Then the hammering. Read verse 27 aloud and the sound of it is the point: he sank, he fell, he lay still... he sank, he fell... where he sank, there he fell. The lines beat like a mallet on a peg, and the last word in the stanza is the last word about Sisera.

'"Out of the window she peered, the mother of Sisera wailed through the lattice: 'Why is his chariot so long in coming? Why tarry the hoofbeats of his chariots?'"'

Now the song does something no reader expects. It leaves the battlefield, crosses into enemy country, and stops at a window.

A woman is watching a road. Her son is late. She has been standing there long enough to start saying it out loud, and the poem lets us hear a mother's voice asking why the chariots have not come back.

We know why. She does not. It is one of the most humane moments in the Old Testament and it was written by the winning side on the day of the victory.

'"Her wisest princesses answer, indeed, she answers herself, 'Have they not found and divided the spoil? — A womb or two for every man; spoil of dyed materials for Sisera...'"'

Then the reassurance she settles on, and it is the ugliest line in the song.

The delay is explained, she decides, by the sharing out of plunder — and the first item on the list is women. A womb or two for every man, in the crudest available Hebrew. Her comfort is that her son is late because his soldiers are dividing up captured girls.

That is a mother saying it, at a window, to steady herself. And it tells the reader exactly what the army in the valley had been doing in the villages for twenty years, and what the empty highways of verse 6 were about.

The song makes us pity her and then shows us what she is comfortable with, in the space of three verses.

verseByVerse.ref: v. 31 — Like the Sun as He Rises
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The song ends in one sentence of prayer and one of report. So may all your enemies perish, O LORD! But your friends be like the sun as he rises in his might. And then the narrator's line: the land had rest for forty years (v. 31).
verseByVerse.theology: The two halves of the prayer belong together. It asks for the end of everything opposed to God and for the shining of everything that loves him, and it does not present those as separate wishes.
verseByVerse.examples: Forty years of quiet, and the reader who has been paying attention knows what the next sentence of the book will be. The rest is real, it is dated, and it is the length of one generation.

verseByVerse.quote: "So may all your enemies perish, O LORD! But your friends be like the sun as he rises in his might." And the land had rest for forty years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'"So may all your enemies perish, O LORD! But your friends be like the sun as he rises in his might." And the land had rest for forty years.'

The song ends in prayer, and the two halves of it are one wish.

The first half is hard, and it should not be tidied up: so may all your enemies perish. It is asked immediately after a scene of a bereaved mother, by people who have just seen what these enemies did to their villages. It is not the reflex of the comfortable.

Prayers like this run all through the Psalms and they ask for one thing: that evil should stop — not be managed, not be balanced, but end. Anybody who has looked closely at what was happening on the roads of Galilee in verse 6, or heard what Sisera's mother expected her son to be doing, has felt the force of the request. The last book of the Bible contains the same prayer, asked by people under an altar, and it is answered rather than rebuked (Rev. 6:10).

The second half is the one to take away. But your friends be like the sun as he rises in his might.

It is a sunrise: the first minute of full light after a night, when the sky goes from grey to unbearable and everything on the ground is suddenly visible. That is what the poem asks for the people who love God — not safety, not comfort, not even victory, but that they should be like that.

It is nearly the last line of the song, and the New Testament finishes the thought. Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father (Matt. 13:43).

Then the narrator adds one flat sentence and the singing stops. And the land had rest for forty years.

Forty years of quiet, bought by a woman under a palm tree, a man who had to be fetched, two tribes who went up the heights, a river in spate, and a housewife with a mallet — and every bit of it credited, in the song they sang about it, to the God who came up out of the south with the mountains shaking and the clouds dropping water.

5.theology:
One march, from Sinai to the Kishon. Before a word about Sisera, the song describes God coming up out of Edom with the mountains quaking and the clouds dropping water (vv. 4-5). It is not decoration. The same weather appears again in verse 21, where the river comes down and takes the chariots. The poem is arguing that what happened in that valley was not a lucky storm but an arrival.

What the absent tribes were doing. The song never calls Reuben, Gilead, Dan or Asher cowards or traitors. It simply records their occupations at the time — sheepfolds, distance, ships, landings — and puts that list beside Zebulun, who risked their lives to the death. Reuben's charge is the most searching in the book, because it is not indifference: great searchings of heart, twice over. He took the matter with great seriousness and stayed within earshot of his flocks.

Meroz. The one community cursed in this song is cursed for doing nothing, and cursed by the angel of the LORD, the figure who delivered the covenant lawsuit at Bochim. The wording is repeated for emphasis: they did not come to the help of the LORD against the mighty — as though God required reinforcements, which he did not. And Meroz never appears again in Scripture. No territory, no clan, no descendants. Its entire trace in the Bible is the sentence cursing it for staying home.

Two women at the end. Jael is called most blessed of women, and the only other person in Scripture greeted that way is Mary (Luke 1:42). Then the song crosses into enemy country and stops at a window, where another woman is waiting for the same man and working out why he is late. What she settles on — the men are dividing the spoil, a womb or two for every man — tells the reader exactly what had been happening on those empty highways for twenty years. The poem makes us pity her and then shows us what she is comfortable with, in three verses.
5.examples:
Then: A nation that had been keeping off the main roads for twenty years sang, on the day of its rescue, a song that named the tribes who came and the tribes who did not, cursed a village for staying home, blessed a housewife with a mallet, and paused at the window of the enemy commander's mother.

Now: Reuben is the one to sit with, because he is the most respectable figure in the poem. He did not refuse; he deliberated, at length and in earnest, within hearing of his own business, and the moment passed. The song's question to him is the one to put to yourself about whatever you are currently weighing: what exactly are you sitting among while the searching of heart goes on?

6.title: The Call of Gideon
6.text: <sup>1</sup>The people of Israel did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, and the LORD gave them into the hand of Midian seven years.<sup>2</sup>And the hand of Midian overpowered Israel, and because of Midian the people of Israel made for themselves the dens that are in the mountains and the caves and the strongholds.<sup>3</sup>For whenever the Israelites planted crops, the Midianites and the Amalekites and the people of the East would come up against them.<sup>4</sup>They would encamp against them and devour the produce of the land, as far as Gaza, and leave no sustenance in Israel and no sheep or ox or donkey.<sup>5</sup>For they would come up with their livestock and their tents; they would come like locusts in number—both they and their camels could not be counted—so that they laid waste the land as they came in.<sup>6</sup>And Israel was brought very low because of Midian. And the people of Israel cried out for help to the LORD.<sup>7</sup>When the people of Israel cried out to the LORD on account of the Midianites,<sup>8</sup>the LORD sent a prophet to the people of Israel. And he said to them, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: I led you up from Egypt and brought you out of the house of slavery.<sup>9</sup>And I delivered you from the hand of the Egyptians and from the hand of all who oppressed you, and drove them out before you and gave you their land.<sup>10</sup>And I said to you, 'I am the LORD your God; you shall not fear the gods of the Amorites in whose land you dwell.' But you have not obeyed my voice."<sup>11</sup>Now the angel of the LORD came and sat under the terebinth at Ophrah, which belonged to Joash the Abiezrite, while his son Gideon was beating out wheat in the winepress to hide it from the Midianites.<sup>12</sup>And the angel of the LORD appeared to him and said to him, "The LORD is with you, O mighty man of valor."<sup>13</sup>And Gideon said to him, "Please, my lord, if the LORD is with us, why then has all this happened to us? And where are all his wonderful deeds that our fathers recounted to us, saying, 'Did not the LORD bring us up from Egypt?' But now the LORD has forsaken us and given us into the hand of Midian."<sup>14</sup>And the LORD turned to him and said, "Go in this might of yours and save Israel from the hand of Midian; do not I send you?"<sup>15</sup>And he said to him, "Please, Lord, how can I save Israel? Behold, my clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father's house."<sup>16</sup>And the LORD said to him, "But I will be with you, and you shall strike the Midianites as one man."<sup>17</sup>And he said to him, "If now I have found favor in your eyes, then show me a sign that it is you who speak with me.<sup>18</sup>Please do not depart from here until I come to you and bring out my present and set it before you." And he said, "I will stay till you return."<sup>19</sup>So Gideon went into his house and prepared a young goat and unleavened cakes from an ephah of flour. The meat he put in a basket, and the broth he put in a pot, and brought them to him under the terebinth and presented them.<sup>20</sup>And the angel of God said to him, "Take the meat and the unleavened cakes, and put them on this rock, and pour the broth over them." And he did so.<sup>21</sup>Then the angel of the LORD reached out the tip of the staff that was in his hand and touched the meat and the unleavened cakes. And fire sprang up from the rock and consumed the meat and the unleavened cakes. And the angel of the LORD vanished from his sight.<sup>22</sup>Then Gideon perceived that he was the angel of the LORD. And Gideon said, "Alas, O Lord GOD! For now I have seen the angel of the LORD face to face."<sup>23</sup>But the LORD said to him, "Peace be to you. Do not fear; you shall not die."<sup>24</sup>Then Gideon built an altar there to the LORD and called it, The LORD Is Peace. To this day it still stands at Ophrah, which belongs to the Abiezrites.<sup>25</sup>That night the LORD said to him, "Take your father's bull, and the second bull seven years old, and pull down the altar of Baal that your father has, and cut down the Asherah that is beside it<sup>26</sup>and build an altar to the LORD your God on the top of the stronghold here, with stones laid in due order. Then take the second bull and offer it as a burnt offering with the wood of the Asherah that you shall cut down."<sup>27</sup>So Gideon took ten men of his servants and did as the LORD had told him. But because he was too afraid of his family and the men of the town to do it by day, he did it by night.<sup>28</sup>When the men of the town rose early in the morning, behold, the altar of Baal was broken down, and the Asherah beside it was cut down, and the second bull was offered on the altar that had been built.<sup>29</sup>And they said to one another, "Who has done this thing?" And after they had searched and inquired, they said, "Gideon the son of Joash has done this thing."<sup>30</sup>Then the men of the town said to Joash, "Bring out your son, that he may die, for he has broken down the altar of Baal and cut down the Asherah beside it."<sup>31</sup>But Joash said to all who stood against him, "Will you contend for Baal? Or will you save him? Whoever contends for him shall be put to death by morning. If he is a god, let him contend for himself, because his altar has been broken down."<sup>32</sup>Therefore on that day Gideon was called Jerubbaal, that is to say, "Let Baal contend against him," because he broke down his altar.<sup>33</sup>Now all the Midianites and the Amalekites and the people of the East came together, and they crossed the Jordan and encamped in the Valley of Jezreel.<sup>34</sup>But the Spirit of the LORD clothed Gideon, and he sounded the trumpet, and the Abiezrites were called out to follow him.<sup>35</sup>And he sent messengers throughout all Manasseh, and they too were called out to follow him. And he sent messengers to Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali, and they went up to meet them.<sup>36</sup>Then Gideon said to God, "If you will save Israel by my hand, as you have said,<sup>37</sup>behold, I am laying a fleece of wool on the threshing floor. If there is dew on the fleece alone, and it is dry on all the ground, then I shall know that you will save Israel by my hand, as you have said."<sup>38</sup>And it was so. When he rose early next morning and squeezed the fleece, he wrung enough dew from the fleece to fill a bowl with water.<sup>39</sup>Then Gideon said to God, "Let not your anger burn against me; let me speak just once more. Please let me test just once more with the fleece. Please let it be dry on the fleece only, and on all the ground let there be dew."<sup>40</sup>And God did so that night; and it was dry on the fleece only, and on all the ground there was dew.
6.overview:
The seventh year of Midian, and Israel is living in caves. Not because the towns have fallen but because the raiders come at harvest — every year Israel is left to plough and sow and tend the crop, and every year, when it is ready to cut, the camels arrive like locusts and take the grain and then the plough animals with it. A whole year of work, annually, for somebody else.

They cry out, and God's first answer is not a rescuer but a preacher. An unnamed prophet arrives, recites what God has done, quotes the command they were given, and leaves the charge standing — but you have not obeyed my voice. No promise, no comfort, and he is never mentioned again. Israel wanted the raids to stop; God answered the real problem before the stated one.

Then the angel of the LORD sits down under a tree and greets a young man threshing wheat in a winepress — a stone pit with no wind in it, the worst possible place for the job, chosen because he is hiding — with the words the LORD is with you, O mighty man of valor. Gideon's objection is accurate and irrelevant, and the answer he gets is the one Moses got at the bush: but I will be with you.

What follows is God's patience, at length. Fire out of a rock. Peace be to you to a man who expected to die. A night raid on his own father's Baal altar, carried out in the dark because he was afraid, and recorded as obedience anyway. The Spirit clothing itself with him. And then, after all of it, a fleece — twice.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Locusts, Caves, and a Sermon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel does evil and God gives them to Midian for seven years (v. 1). The oppression is agricultural and calculated: raiders come up every harvest with the Amalekites and the people of the East, camp on the crop, and strip the country as far as Gaza, leaving no sustenance and no animals (vv. 3-4). They come like locusts, they and their camels beyond counting (v. 5). Israel takes to dens, caves and mountain strongholds (v. 2), is brought very low, and cries out (v. 6). And God's first answer is not a rescuer: he sends a prophet, who recites what God has done, quotes the command they were given, and leaves the charge standing — but you have not obeyed my voice (vv. 7-10).
verseByVerse.theology: The raiding is timed. Israel is allowed to plough, sow and tend a crop all year, and the Midianites arrive when it is ready. That is worse than simple conquest; it turns every season of work into a season of dread.
verseByVerse.examples: The prophet is unnamed, brings no promise, and is never mentioned again. He arrives between the crying out and the rescue, says only what the angel said at Bochim, and goes. Israel wanted the pain to stop and God sent them a diagnosis first.

verseByVerse.quote: The people of Israel did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, and the LORD gave them into the hand of Midian seven years. And the hand of Midian overpowered Israel, and because of Midian the people of Israel made for themselves the dens that are in the mountains and the caves and the strongholds. For whenever the Israelites planted crops, the Midianites and the Amalekites and the people of the East would come up against them. They would encamp against them and devour the produce of the land, as far as Gaza, and leave no sustenance in Israel and no sheep or ox or donkey. For they would come up with their livestock and their tents; they would come like locusts in number—both they and their camels could not be counted—so that they laid waste the land as they came in. And Israel was brought very low because of Midian. And the people of Israel cried out for help to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'The people of Israel did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, and the LORD gave them into the hand of Midian seven years. And the hand of Midian overpowered Israel, and because of Midian the people of Israel made for themselves the dens that are in the mountains and the caves and the strongholds.'

Picture what verse 2 describes. God's people, in the land God swore to give them, living underground.

Not in the walled towns and not on the farms — in dens, caves and strongholds up in the hills. A generation earlier the complaint was about towns not taken; now Israelites are digging holes to sleep in on ground that is legally theirs.

'For whenever the Israelites planted crops, the Midianites and the Amalekites and the people of the East would come up against them. They would encamp against them and devour the produce of the land, as far as Gaza, and leave no sustenance in Israel and no sheep or ox or donkey.'

The oppression is agricultural, and the timing is the cruelty. This is not an invasion; it is an annual harvest.

Israel is left alone to plough in the winter, sow in the spring, weed, water and watch the crop come up. Then, when it is ready to cut, the raiders arrive and camp on it. Everything is taken — the grain, and then the sheep and the oxen and the donkeys, which means next year's ploughing as well.

A whole year of labour, every year, done for somebody else. That is a particular kind of misery: not the terror of a battle but the slow exhaustion of working hard at something you already know you will not keep.

'For they would come up with their livestock and their tents; they would come like locusts in number — both they and their camels could not be counted — so that they laid waste the land as they came in.'

Two details in that verse explain how it was possible. The first is the comparison: locusts. Not an army but a swarm, arriving in a season, eating everything green and moving on.

The second is the camels, and this is the earliest appearance in the Bible of camels used at this scale in war. A camel raid could cross desert that horses could not, cover ground fast, appear where nobody was watching and be gone before a defence could form. Israel had no answer to it and no way even to find them.

'And Israel was brought very low because of Midian. And the people of Israel cried out for help to the LORD.'

They cry out. As always in this book, it is not called repentance; they are hungry and frightened and they make a noise.

verseByVerse.quote: When the people of Israel cried out to the LORD on account of the Midianites, the LORD sent a prophet to the people of Israel. And he said to them, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: I led you up from Egypt and brought you out of the house of slavery. And I delivered you from the hand of the Egyptians and from the hand of all who oppressed you, and drove them out before you and gave you their land. And I said to you, 'I am the LORD your God; you shall not fear the gods of the Amorites in whose land you dwell.' But you have not obeyed my voice."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'When the people of Israel cried out to the LORD on account of the Midianites, the LORD sent a prophet to the people of Israel.'

This is the surprise of the chapter, and it is easy to read past.

Every previous cycle has run the same way: they cried out, and the LORD raised up a deliverer. Here they cry out and God sends a preacher.

'And he said to them, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: I led you up from Egypt and brought you out of the house of slavery. And I delivered you from the hand of the Egyptians and from the hand of all who oppressed you, and drove them out before you and gave you their land."'

The sermon is a recital of what God has done, in the first person, exactly as at Bochim. Four verbs, all his: I led you up, I brought you out, I delivered, I drove them out. And one gift: I gave you their land.

'"And I said to you, 'I am the LORD your God; you shall not fear the gods of the Amorites in whose land you dwell.' But you have not obeyed my voice."'

Then the command, and then the charge, and the charge is the same six words the angel used in 2:2. Nothing new is being said. Israel is simply being told again what it already knew.

Mark what the prophet does not bring. There is no promise, no comfort, no announcement that help is on the way. He states the case and stops, and he is not named and never appears again.

That silence is deliberate, and it is a kindness rather than a cruelty. Israel's cry so far is the cry of people who want the raids to stop; it says nothing about Baal. God's first answer to a prayer for relief is a sermon about the cause, because a rescue delivered into an unchanged situation would only have started the clock on the next seven years.

The prophet's arrival is God taking the crying out seriously enough to answer the real problem rather than the stated one.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–24 — The LORD Is with You, Mighty Man of Valour
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The angel of the LORD sits down under a tree at Ophrah while Gideon threshes wheat in a winepress to hide it (v. 11), and greets him: the LORD is with you, O mighty man of valor (v. 12). Gideon's answer is a complaint — if the LORD is with us, why has all this happened, and where are the wonderful deeds our fathers told us about (v. 13)? He is sent anyway (v. 14), objects that his clan is the weakest and he is the least in his father's house (v. 15), and is answered with one promise: but I will be with you (v. 16). He asks for a sign, brings out a meal, and fire comes up out of the rock and eats it (vv. 17-21). Then he is terrified for his life, and hears peace be to you (vv. 22-23), and builds an altar and calls it The LORD Is Peace (v. 24).
verseByVerse.theology: A winepress is a pit cut in rock, with no wind in it. Threshing wheat there is doing the right job in the worst possible place, and the reason is given: to hide it from the Midianites. The angel walks up to a frightened man in a hole and calls him a mighty man of valour.
verseByVerse.examples: The exchange in verses 15-16 has happened once before, at a bush in the desert. Moses said who am I that I should go? and was answered but I will be with you (Ex. 3:11-12). Neither man is told he is capable. Both are told who is coming with them.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the angel of the LORD came and sat under the terebinth at Ophrah, which belonged to Joash the Abiezrite, while his son Gideon was beating out wheat in the winepress to hide it from the Midianites. And the angel of the LORD appeared to him and said to him, "The LORD is with you, O mighty man of valor."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now the angel of the LORD came and sat under the terebinth at Ophrah, which belonged to Joash the Abiezrite, while his son Gideon was beating out wheat in the winepress to hide it from the Midianites.'

Two men are in this verse and neither is doing what he should be. The angel of the LORD is sitting under a tree; Gideon is threshing wheat in a hole in the ground.

The detail is precise and it needs unpacking. Wheat was threshed on a threshing floor: a flat open place, deliberately sited on a rise, because the whole process depends on wind. You beat the grain out and then throw it up so the breeze carries the chaff away.

A winepress is the opposite of that in every respect. It is a pit cut down into rock, out of the wind, where grapes were trodden. Nothing about it works for threshing wheat, and the writer tells us why he is doing it anyway: to hide it from the Midianites.

So the picture is a young man crouched in a stone pit, doing a job badly in the one place it cannot be done well, because the alternative is being seen. He is not fighting anybody. He is saving a few bushels of grain from the swarm.

'And the angel of the LORD appeared to him and said to him, "The LORD is with you, O mighty man of valor."'

That is what God's messenger says to him.

Both halves of the greeting look wrong. The LORD is with you, said to a man in a hole in an occupied country; and O mighty man of valour, said to somebody hiding his breakfast.

The phrase is gibbor hayil, and it is a real title — used of soldiers of proven courage and of men of substance in a community. It is the last description anybody in Ophrah would have applied to Gideon that afternoon, including Gideon.

God is not flattering him and he is not being ironic. He is naming what this man is going to be, before there is any evidence for it, and the naming is the first act of the making.

verseByVerse.quote: And Gideon said to him, "Please, my lord, if the LORD is with us, why then has all this happened to us? And where are all his wonderful deeds that our fathers recounted to us, saying, 'Did not the LORD bring us up from Egypt?' But now the LORD has forsaken us and given us into the hand of Midian." And the LORD turned to him and said, "Go in this might of yours and save Israel from the hand of Midian; do not I send you?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And Gideon said to him, "Please, my lord, if the LORD is with us, why then has all this happened to us? And where are all his wonderful deeds that our fathers recounted to us, saying, 'Did not the LORD bring us up from Egypt?' But now the LORD has forsaken us and given us into the hand of Midian."'

Gideon does not thank the messenger for the compliment. He argues with the first half of it, and the argument is the honest complaint of a man who has been reading his circumstances.

Now hold this verse against 2:10, because Gideon is the opposite problem. There the tragedy was a generation that did not know the LORD or the work that he had done. Gideon knows the work. He can quote it — the wonderful deeds that our fathers recounted to us, and he knows the sentence that goes with them: did not the LORD bring us up from Egypt?

The stories got through to him. Somebody answered the question at Gilgal after all. And he has looked at the stories, looked at the winepress, and concluded that they belong to different worlds.

That is a distinct kind of unbelief and a very common one. It is not ignorance and it is not denial. It is a man who believes every word of what God did and has quietly stopped expecting anything of the sort now — who reads his own circumstances as the more recent and reliable evidence.

His conclusion is a serious charge: the LORD has forsaken us. It is also, in this book, precisely wrong. What has happened to Israel is not abandonment; chapter 2 said God gave them over, sold them, was against them for harm. Gideon has mistaken discipline for desertion.

'And the LORD turned to him and said, "Go in this might of yours and save Israel from the hand of Midian; do not I send you?"'

The reply does not answer a single one of his questions.

God does not defend himself, explain the seven years, or produce a theology of suffering. He gives the man a job.

And the phrase is deliberately puzzling: go in this might of yours. What might? The only thing Gideon has demonstrated is the ability to hide grain and complain accurately. The sentence is either mockery or a promise about what is now in him, and the question that follows settles which: do not I send you?

The whole commission rests on the sending. Not on the strength, which is not there, but on the one who is doing the sending.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, "Please, Lord, how can I save Israel? Behold, my clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father's house." And the LORD said to him, "But I will be with you, and you shall strike the Midianites as one man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And he said to him, "Please, Lord, how can I save Israel? Behold, my clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father's house."'

His objection is not false modesty. It is an accurate report.

He gives two facts, and each is a step down. Manasseh is a middling tribe; within it his clan is the weakest; within the clan he is the youngest and least in his own father's household. He is at the bottom of a small heap, and everything he says is true.

What is wrong with it is the first four words: how can I save Israel? The question assumes the saving depends on his resources, and on that assumption the inventory is decisive.

'And the LORD said to him, "But I will be with you, and you shall strike the Midianites as one man."'

God does not argue with the inventory. He does not tell Gideon that he has hidden potential, that Manasseh is stronger than he thinks, or that the least in a household often surprises people. Every fact Gideon has stated is allowed to stand.

The answer is one clause: but I will be with you.

This exchange has happened before, word for word in substance, at a burning bush on the far side of a desert. Moses said, who am I that I should go to Pharaoh? and God answered, but I will be with you (Ex. 3:11-12). The question was about the man; the answer was about God, and it did not engage with the question at all.

That is the shape of every genuine call in Scripture. The objection is usually correct and always irrelevant. Nobody in the Bible is ever told that he is equal to what he is being asked to do.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, "If now I have found favor in your eyes, then show me a sign that it is you who speak with me. Please do not depart from here until I come to you and bring out my present and set it before you." And he said, "I will stay till you return." So Gideon went into his house and prepared a young goat and unleavened cakes from an ephah of flour. The meat he put in a basket, and the broth he put in a pot, and brought them to him under the terebinth and presented them. And the angel of God said to him, "Take the meat and the unleavened cakes, and put them on this rock, and pour the broth over them." And he did so. Then the angel of the LORD reached out the tip of the staff that was in his hand and touched the meat and the unleavened cakes. And fire sprang up from the rock and consumed the meat and the unleavened cakes. And the angel of the LORD vanished from his sight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And he said to him, "If now I have found favor in your eyes, then show me a sign that it is you who speak with me. Please do not depart from here until I come to you and bring out my present and set it before you."'

He asks for a sign, and then asks the visitor to wait while he goes and gets something.

'So Gideon went into his house and prepared a young goat and unleavened cakes from an ephah of flour. The meat he put in a basket, and the broth he put in a pot, and brought them to him under the terebinth and presented them.'

Take in what he brings out, in the seventh year of a famine caused by raiders who leave no sustenance in Israel. A whole young goat. An ephah of flour, which is something like twenty pounds — the amount Abraham had Sarah bake for the three visitors at Mamre.

Gideon has been threshing in a pit to save a little grain, and he takes a large part of what his household has and cooks it for a stranger under a tree. Whatever is wrong with his faith, his hospitality is not calculating.

'And the angel of God said to him, "Take the meat and the unleavened cakes, and put them on this rock, and pour the broth over them." And he did so.'

The instruction turns a meal into an offering. Meat and bread on a rock, and then the broth poured over the lot, which soaks everything and makes it very much harder to burn.

'Then the angel of the LORD reached out the tip of the staff that was in his hand and touched the meat and the unleavened cakes. And fire sprang up from the rock and consumed the meat and the unleavened cakes. And the angel of the LORD vanished from his sight.'

The staff touches it and fire comes out of the rock — not down from the sky, but up through the stone under the food. It burns a soaked meal to nothing, and the visitor is gone.

The sign Gideon asked for was proof of identity, and what he gets is fire out of the ground and an empty space under the tree.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Gideon perceived that he was the angel of the LORD. And Gideon said, "Alas, O Lord GOD! For now I have seen the angel of the LORD face to face." But the LORD said to him, "Peace be to you. Do not fear; you shall not die." Then Gideon built an altar there to the LORD and called it, The LORD Is Peace. To this day it still stands at Ophrah, which belongs to the Abiezrites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Gideon perceived that he was the angel of the LORD. And Gideon said, "Alas, O Lord GOD! For now I have seen the angel of the LORD face to face."'

The proof he asked for arrives, and the first thing it produces in him is terror.

He is not frightened of Midian in this verse. He is frightened because he has been talking face to face with somebody he now understands, and the conviction ran deep in Israel that this kills a man. God had told Moses plainly: you cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live (Ex. 33:20). Jacob, after wrestling all night at Peniel, said the same in astonishment: I have seen God face to face, and yet my life has been delivered (Gen. 32:30).

Gideon's terror is not superstition. It is the correct instinct of a man who has just realised who was sitting under the tree while he complained about the state of the country.

'But the LORD said to him, "Peace be to you. Do not fear; you shall not die."'

Three short sentences, and they are the gospel in the order the gospel always comes.

Peace first, then the command not to be afraid, then the reason. And nothing in Gideon has changed between his terror and this answer. He has not offered anything, promised anything or improved. The word is simply spoken over him.

'Then Gideon built an altar there to the LORD and called it, The LORD Is Peace. To this day it still stands at Ophrah, which belongs to the Abiezrites.'

He builds an altar and names it after the sentence that saved his life: YHWH Shalom, the LORD Is Peace.

It is a strange name for a man about to fight a war, and it is the right one. What Gideon has just discovered is not that God is on his side against Midian. It is that God is at peace with him — a frightened man from the least family of the weakest clan, who had spent the afternoon accusing God of desertion.

The stone was still standing when the book was written, and centuries later Paul would put the same word at the centre of everything, and make it a person rather than an altar: for he himself is our peace (Eph. 2:14).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–32 — The Altar in His Father's Yard
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: That same night the orders come, and they are domestic: pull down the altar of Baal that your father has, cut down the Asherah beside it, build an altar to the LORD, and offer the second bull — the seven-year-old — on the wood of the Asherah pole (vv. 25-26). Gideon takes ten servants and does it, and the narrator does not cover for him: he did it by night, because he was too afraid of his family and the town to do it by day (v. 27). In the morning the town wants him dead (vv. 28-30), and the man who defends him is his father, the owner of the altar: if he is a god, let him contend for himself (v. 31). So they nickname Gideon Jerubbaal, let Baal contend against him (v. 32).
verseByVerse.theology: Before Gideon is sent against Midian he is sent against his own father's back garden. The war with the external enemy waits on the demolition of the household idol, and the household is his.
verseByVerse.examples: The bull is seven years old and the oppression has lasted seven years (v. 1). The animal that goes onto the fire was born in the year the trouble started, and it is burned with the wood of the idol that caused it.

verseByVerse.quote: That night the LORD said to him, "Take your father's bull, and the second bull seven years old, and pull down the altar of Baal that your father has, and cut down the Asherah that is beside it and build an altar to the LORD your God on the top of the stronghold here, with stones laid in due order. Then take the second bull and offer it as a burnt offering with the wood of the Asherah that you shall cut down." So Gideon took ten men of his servants and did as the LORD had told him. But because he was too afraid of his family and the men of the town to do it by day, he did it by night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'That night the LORD said to him, "Take your father's bull, and the second bull seven years old, and pull down the altar of Baal that your father has, and cut down the Asherah that is beside it."'

The first assignment is not Midian. It is his father's back garden.

Read the phrase again: the altar of Baal that your father has. Joash the Abiezrite, the man who owns the field where the angel sat, maintains a shrine to Baal, with an Asherah pole next to it. The chapter has just told us Israel cried out to the LORD in their distress; this is where the family went the rest of the year.

So before Gideon can be sent against the raiders, he is sent against the household. There is no chance of Israel being delivered from Midian while the deliverer's own father runs a Baal altar, and God begins where the young man actually lives.

The animal is specified: the second bull, seven years old. Go back to verse 1, where the LORD gave Israel into the hand of Midian for seven years. That bull was born in the year the raids began. It has grown up alongside the oppression, and it is about to be burned on the wood of the idol that caused it.

'"and build an altar to the LORD your God on the top of the stronghold here, with stones laid in due order. Then take the second bull and offer it as a burnt offering with the wood of the Asherah that you shall cut down."'

The Asherah pole becomes firewood for the sacrifice. Nothing is left standing and nothing is wasted; the idol heats the offering that replaces it.

'So Gideon took ten men of his servants and did as the LORD had told him. But because he was too afraid of his family and the men of the town to do it by day, he did it by night.'

The narrator will not tidy him up.

He did it. Ten servants, the altar down, the pole cut, the bull offered — every instruction carried out. And he did it in the dark because he was frightened of his own family and his own neighbours.

Both halves are recorded and neither cancels the other. This is obedience with the hands shaking, and Scripture calls it obedience. There is no suggestion that God wanted it done again in daylight, and no rebuke anywhere in the chapter.

Say it plainly, because a great deal of Christian courage looks like this from the inside. The command is obeyed and the fear is real at the same time, and the fear does not disqualify the obedience.

verseByVerse.quote: When the men of the town rose early in the morning, behold, the altar of Baal was broken down, and the Asherah beside it was cut down, and the second bull was offered on the altar that had been built. And they said to one another, "Who has done this thing?" And after they had searched and inquired, they said, "Gideon the son of Joash has done this thing." Then the men of the town said to Joash, "Bring out your son, that he may die, for he has broken down the altar of Baal and cut down the Asherah beside it." But Joash said to all who stood against him, "Will you contend for Baal? Or will you save him? Whoever contends for him shall be put to death by morning. If he is a god, let him contend for himself, because his altar has been broken down." Therefore on that day Gideon was called Jerubbaal, that is to say, "Let Baal contend against him," because he broke down his altar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'When the men of the town rose early in the morning, behold, the altar of Baal was broken down, and the Asherah beside it was cut down, and the second bull was offered on the altar that had been built.'

The town wakes up to find its shrine demolished and a sacrifice already burning on a new altar built out of the wreckage.

'And they said to one another, "Who has done this thing?" And after they had searched and inquired, they said, "Gideon the son of Joash has done this thing." Then the men of the town said to Joash, "Bring out your son, that he may die, for he has broken down the altar of Baal."'

They investigate, they find him, and they come for a death sentence.

Look carefully at who these men are. They are Israelites. They are the same people who were crying out to the LORD in verse 6 because the Midianites were eating their harvest, and they are now demanding capital punishment for a man who pulled down a Canaanite altar.

That is how far it has gone. The nation prays to the God of the exodus when the raiders come and lynches anyone who interferes with Baal.

'But Joash said to all who stood against him, "Will you contend for Baal? Or will you save him? Whoever contends for him shall be put to death by morning. If he is a god, let him contend for himself, because his altar has been broken down."'

The defence comes from the last man anybody would expect: Joash, who owned the altar.

His argument is unanswerable and it takes one sentence. If he is a god, let him contend for himself.

Turn it over and see how much it demolishes. A god who requires a mob to defend his honour has already lost the argument. If Baal is what the town says he is, he is perfectly capable of dealing with one young man overnight; if he needs the men of Ophrah to do it for him, he is not worth the altar they are avenging.

It is the same case Elijah will make on Carmel with heavier irony, and the same case Isaiah will make about men who cut down a tree, burn half of it and pray to the other half. A god you have to protect is not a god.

'Therefore on that day Gideon was called Jerubbaal, that is to say, "Let Baal contend against him," because he broke down his altar.'

He gets a nickname out of it, and it is a standing dare: let Baal contend. Every time somebody says the name, the challenge is repeated and Baal's silence is noted again. Gideon carries that name for the rest of his life, and his sons carry it after him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The whole confederation crosses the Jordan and camps in the valley of Jezreel (v. 33). Then the sentence that changes Gideon: the Spirit of the LORD clothed Gideon, and he blows a trumpet and four tribes come (vv. 34-35). And then, after the angel, the fire, the altar and the Spirit, he asks for another sign — a fleece wet with dew on dry ground (vv. 36-37). God does it (v. 38). Gideon asks for the reverse, apologising as he asks (v. 39), and God does that too (v. 40).
verseByVerse.theology: The Hebrew in verse 34 is unusual and worth having exactly: the Spirit of the LORD clothed himself with Gideon. The man is not given a power to use; he is put on like a garment by somebody else.
verseByVerse.examples: The second test is the intelligent one, and it is the reason to be slower in mocking him. Wool left out overnight will draw dew and hold it while the ground round it dries — the first test could have happened on its own. The reverse cannot. Gideon spotted the flaw in his own experiment and asked for the one result nature does not produce.

verseByVerse.quote: Now all the Midianites and the Amalekites and the people of the East came together, and they crossed the Jordan and encamped in the Valley of Jezreel. But the Spirit of the LORD clothed Gideon, and he sounded the trumpet, and the Abiezrites were called out to follow him. And he sent messengers throughout all Manasseh, and they too were called out to follow him. And he sent messengers to Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali, and they went up to meet them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now all the Midianites and the Amalekites and the people of the East came together, and they crossed the Jordan and encamped in the Valley of Jezreel.'

The whole confederation crosses over and camps in the great plain — the same valley where the Kishon took Sisera's chariots two chapters ago. They are not raiding this time. They have come to stay.

'But the Spirit of the LORD clothed Gideon, and he sounded the trumpet, and the Abiezrites were called out to follow him.'

Here is the sentence that changes him, and the Hebrew is unusual enough to be worth having exactly. It does not say the Spirit came upon Gideon, as with Othniel. It says the Spirit of the LORD clothed himself with Gideon — put him on, the way a man puts on a coat.

Gideon is not handed an ability to deploy. He is worn.

The same phrase is used twice more in the Old Testament, both times of the Spirit taking hold of a man so that he speaks or acts beyond himself (1 Chron. 12:18; 2 Chron. 24:20). It is the only explanation offered for what happens next.

'And he sent messengers throughout all Manasseh, and they too were called out to follow him. And he sent messengers to Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali, and they went up to meet them.'

The man who was hiding grain in a pit that morning blows a trumpet and summons four tribes, and they come.

Nothing about his circumstances has altered. His clan is still the weakest in Manasseh and he is still the least in his father's house; the inventory in verse 15 was accurate and remains accurate. What has changed is who is wearing him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Gideon said to God, "If you will save Israel by my hand, as you have said, behold, I am laying a fleece of wool on the threshing floor. If there is dew on the fleece alone, and it is dry on all the ground, then I shall know that you will save Israel by my hand, as you have said." And it was so. When he rose early next morning and squeezed the fleece, he wrung enough dew from the fleece to fill a bowl with water. Then Gideon said to God, "Let not your anger burn against me; let me speak just once more. Please let me test just once more with the fleece. Please let it be dry on the fleece only, and on all the ground let there be dew." And God did so that night; and it was dry on the fleece only, and on all the ground there was dew.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Gideon said to God, "If you will save Israel by my hand, as you have said, behold, I am laying a fleece of wool on the threshing floor. If there is dew on the fleece alone, and it is dry on all the ground, then I shall know that you will save Israel by my hand, as you have said."'

Take stock of what this man has already been given before he asks for this.

An angel of the LORD, in person, under a tree. A commission spoken directly to him. The promise I will be with you. Fire out of a rock. The word peace be to you when he expected to die. An altar he built himself and named. A night raid carried out and survived. And the Spirit of the LORD wrapped round him like clothing.

Then he lays out a fleece.

Mark how he phrases it, twice: as you have said. He is not asking whether God said it; he is asking whether God meant it. The request is not for information. It is for reassurance.

'And it was so. When he rose early next morning and squeezed the fleece, he wrung enough dew from the fleece to fill a bowl with water.'

God does it, without comment. A bowlful of water out of the wool, and dry ground all round it.

'Then Gideon said to God, "Let not your anger burn against me; let me speak just once more. Please let me test just once more with the fleece. Please let it be dry on the fleece only, and on all the ground let there be dew."'

He asks again, and the way he asks tells us he knows exactly what he is doing. Let not your anger burn against me is the language of a man apologising in advance, and it is almost word for word what Abraham said when he kept reducing the number for Sodom (Gen. 18:30, 32).

Now here is the thing that should slow anybody down before mocking him. His second test is the intelligent one.

A fleece of wool left out overnight will draw dew and hold it while the ground round it dries in the first sun; wool does that, and any shepherd knows it. The first test could have happened by itself. The reverse — dry wool on wet ground — cannot.

Gideon spotted the flaw in his own experiment and asked for the one result that nature does not produce. He is not being lazily superstitious. He is being careful, and his carefulness exposes how much he still needs.

'And God did so that night; and it was dry on the fleece only, and on all the ground there was dew.'

God does that too.

Five words, no rebuke, no lecture about the signs already given, no weary sigh in the text at all. The God who had already appeared to this man in person, spoken to him, set a rock on fire for him and clothed himself with him, gets up in the night and does the second experiment.

This is not a method to copy, and the chapter is not recommending fleeces. Gideon was not seeking guidance he lacked; he was seeking confidence in guidance he already had, and every reader who has ever asked God for one more confirmation of something already perfectly clear knows precisely which of the two he was doing.

What the passage is recommending is its God. He does not break a bruised reed or quench a smouldering wick (Isa. 42:3), and here is what that looks like in practice: a frightened man asking for the same assurance twice in two nights, and getting it twice, from the one who had already called him a mighty man of valour while he was hiding in a hole.

6.theology:
Named for what he will be. Mighty man of valor is a real title, used of proven soldiers and men of standing, and it is spoken to somebody hiding grain in a pit. God is not flattering him and not being ironic; he is naming what this man will become before there is any evidence for it, and the naming is the first act of the making.

The objection is correct and irrelevant. Gideon's inventory in verse 15 is accurate — weakest clan, least in the house — and God does not dispute a word of it. The answer is one clause, but I will be with you, and it is the same answer Moses received at the burning bush to the same question (Ex. 3:11-12). Nobody in Scripture is ever told he is equal to what he is being asked to do.

Knowing the stories is not enough either. Chapter 2 described a generation that did not know the work God had done. Gideon is the opposite case: he can quote the wonderful deeds his fathers recounted, and he has weighed them against the winepress and concluded that God has forsaken them (v. 13). That is not ignorance and not denial. It is a man who believes the history and has stopped expecting anything like it now — and he has mistaken discipline for desertion.

Obedience with the hands shaking. Gideon pulls down his father's altar exactly as commanded, and does it at night because he was too afraid to do it by day (v. 27). Both halves are recorded, neither cancels the other, and there is no rebuke anywhere. Nor is there one for the fleece, asked for after an angel, a fire, an altar and the Spirit — and asked twice. The God of this chapter does not break a bruised reed or quench a smouldering wick (Isa. 42:3), and verse 40 is what that looks like on the ground.
6.examples:
Then: A young man from the least family of the weakest clan was crouched in a winepress saving a few bushels of wheat from raiders when somebody sat down under the tree above him and called him a mighty man of valour. Before he was sent against an army he was sent against his own father's shrine, and he did it after dark because he was frightened.

Now: Two things. The first is verse 13, and it is the more searching of the two: it is possible to know exactly what God has done, to be able to recite it, and to have quietly concluded from your own circumstances that he has stopped. Gideon had the stories. What he had lost was the expectation. The second is verse 27 — if you are waiting to stop being afraid before you obey, this chapter records a man who obeyed at night instead, and God did not mention it again.

7.title: Gideon's 300
7.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Jerubbaal (that is, Gideon) and all the people who were with him rose early and encamped beside the spring of Harod. And the camp of Midian was north of them, by the hill of Moreh, in the valley.<sup>2</sup>The LORD said to Gideon, "The people with you are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hand, lest Israel boast over me, saying, 'My own hand has saved me.'<sup>3</sup>Now therefore proclaim in the ears of the people, saying, 'Whoever is fearful and trembling, let him return home and hurry away from Mount Gilead.'" Then 22,000 of the people returned, and 10,000 remained.<sup>4</sup>And the LORD said to Gideon, "The people are still too many. Take them down to the water, and I will test them for you there, and anyone of whom I say to you, 'This one shall go with you,' shall go with you, and anyone of whom I say to you, 'This one shall not go with you,' shall not go."<sup>5</sup>So he brought the people down to the water. And the LORD said to Gideon, "Every one who laps the water with his tongue, as a dog laps, you shall set by himself. Likewise, every one who kneels down to drink."<sup>6</sup>And the number of those who lapped, putting their hands to their mouths, was 300 men, but all the rest of the people knelt down to drink water.<sup>7</sup>And the LORD said to Gideon, "With the 300 men who lapped I will save you and give the Midianites into your hand, and let all the others go every man to his home."<sup>8</sup>So the people took provisions in their hands, and their trumpets. And he sent all the rest of Israel every man to his tent, but retained the 300 men. And the camp of Midian was below him in the valley.<sup>9</sup>That same night the LORD said to him, "Arise, go down against the camp, for I have given it into your hand.<sup>10</sup>But if you are afraid to go down, go down to the camp with Purah your servant.<sup>11</sup>And you shall hear what they say, and afterward your hands shall be strengthened to go down against the camp." Then he went down with Purah his servant to the outposts of the armed men who were in the camp.<sup>12</sup>And the Midianites and the Amalekites and all the people of the East lay along the valley like locusts in abundance, and their camels were without number, as the sand that is on the seashore in abundance.<sup>13</sup>When Gideon came, behold, a man was telling a dream to his comrade. And he said, "Behold, I dreamed a dream, and behold, a cake of barley bread tumbled into the camp of Midian and came to the tent and struck it so that it fell and turned it upside down, so that the tent lay flat."<sup>14</sup>And his comrade answered, "This is no other than the sword of Gideon the son of Joash, a man of Israel; God has given into his hand Midian and all the camp."<sup>15</sup>As soon as Gideon heard the telling of the dream and its interpretation, he worshiped. And he returned to the camp of Israel and said, "Arise, for the LORD has given the host of Midian into your hand."<sup>16</sup>And he divided the 300 men into three companies and put trumpets into the hands of all of them and empty jars, with torches inside the jars.<sup>17</sup>And he said to them, "Look at me, and do likewise. When I come to the outskirts of the camp, do as I do.<sup>18</sup>When I blow the trumpet, I and all who are with me, then blow the trumpets also on every side of all the camp and shout, 'For the LORD and for Gideon.'"<sup>19</sup>So Gideon and the hundred men who were with him came to the outskirts of the camp at the beginning of the middle watch, when they had just set the watch. And they blew the trumpets and smashed the jars that were in their hands.<sup>20</sup>Then the three companies blew the trumpets and broke the jars. They held in their left hands the torches, and in their right hands the trumpets to blow. And they cried out, "A sword for the LORD and for Gideon!"<sup>21</sup>Every man stood in his place around the camp, and all the army ran. They cried out and fled.<sup>22</sup>When they blew the 300 trumpets, the LORD set every man's sword against his comrade and against all the army. And the army fled as far as Beth-shittah toward Zererah, as far as the border of Abel-meholah, by Tabbath.<sup>23</sup>And the men of Israel were called out from Naphtali and from Asher and from all Manasseh, and they pursued after Midian.<sup>24</sup>Gideon sent messengers throughout all the hill country of Ephraim, saying, "Come down against the Midianites and capture the waters against them, as far as Beth-barah, and also the Jordan." So all the men of Ephraim were called out, and they captured the waters as far as Beth-barah, and also the Jordan.<sup>25</sup>And they captured the two princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb. They killed Oreb at the rock of Oreb, and Zeeb they killed at the winepress of Zeeb. Then they pursued Midian, and they brought the heads of Oreb and Zeeb to Gideon across the Jordan.
7.overview:
Gideon has thirty-two thousand men and God's objection to the army is that it is too many. Not too small, not badly armed — too many to be a convincing explanation: lest Israel boast over me, saying, My own hand has saved me (v. 2). Everything in the chapter serves that sentence. God is not arranging a victory here so much as an account of it that nobody can misread.

The first cut is Israel's own war law read aloud — anyone fearful may go home (Deut. 20:8) — and twenty-two thousand men take it. The second, at the water, is not explained, and it is better not to make it clever: if the three hundred had been chosen for alertness we would be back at a victory that could be credited to good selection, which verse 2 has already ruled out.

Then the night visit, and the tenderest line in the Gideon story. God says go down, but if you are afraid to go down, go down with Purah your servant (v. 10). Not do not be afraid, and no rebuke for still being frightened after an angel, a fire, the Spirit and two fleeces. He is given a companion and something to overhear — an enemy soldier's dream about a barley loaf, the poor man's bread, the grain these raiders had been stealing for seven years, rolling into the camp and flattening a tent.

The attack itself is three hundred men with a trumpet in one hand and a torch in the other, and no hand left for a weapon. They stand still, make a noise, and the LORD sets every man's sword against his comrade.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Gideon camps at the spring of Harod with Midian in the valley below (v. 1), and God tells him the problem: the people with you are too many — not for the battle, but lest Israel boast over me, saying, My own hand has saved me (v. 2). Whoever is fearful may go home, and twenty-two thousand leave; ten thousand stay (v. 3). Still too many. At the water, three hundred lap from their hands and the rest kneel, and God keeps the three hundred (vv. 4-7). The rest are sent to their tents with the provisions and the trumpets left behind (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: The army is not reduced because it is unfit. It is reduced because it is large enough to be credited. God is not arranging a victory; he is arranging an explanation.
verseByVerse.examples: The offer in verse 3 is not Gideon's idea. Deuteronomy required the officers before battle to send home anyone fearful and fainthearted, so that his fear would not spread (Deut. 20:8). Gideon reads out the standing law, and two thirds of his army takes it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jerubbaal (that is, Gideon) and all the people who were with him rose early and encamped beside the spring of Harod. And the camp of Midian was north of them, by the hill of Moreh, in the valley. The LORD said to Gideon, "The people with you are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hand, lest Israel boast over me, saying, 'My own hand has saved me.' Now therefore proclaim in the ears of the people, saying, 'Whoever is fearful and trembling, let him return home and hurry away from Mount Gilead.'" Then 22,000 of the people returned, and 10,000 remained. And the LORD said to Gideon, "The people are still too many. Take them down to the water, and I will test them for you there, and anyone of whom I say to you, 'This one shall go with you,' shall go with you, and anyone of whom I say to you, 'This one shall not go with you,' shall not go." So he brought the people down to the water. And the LORD said to Gideon, "Every one who laps the water with his tongue, as a dog laps, you shall set by himself. Likewise, every one who kneels down to drink." And the number of those who lapped, putting their hands to their mouths, was 300 men, but all the rest of the people knelt down to drink water. And the LORD said to Gideon, "With the 300 men who lapped I will save you and give the Midianites into your hand, and let all the others go every man to his home." So the people took provisions in their hands, and their trumpets. And he sent all the rest of Israel every man to his tent, but retained the 300 men. And the camp of Midian was below him in the valley.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Jerubbaal (that is, Gideon) and all the people who were with him rose early and encamped beside the spring of Harod. And the camp of Midian was north of them, by the hill of Moreh, in the valley.'

He is called Jerubbaal first — let Baal contend — and the name is a standing dare that Baal has now been ignoring for some time.

'The LORD said to Gideon, "The people with you are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hand, lest Israel boast over me, saying, 'My own hand has saved me.'"'

Here is the sentence the whole chapter exists to serve, and it has nothing to do with tactics.

Gideon has thirty-two thousand men facing a coalition described as locusts, and God's objection to the army is that it is too many. Not too few, not badly equipped, not poorly positioned. Too many to be a convincing explanation.

Read the reason again: lest Israel boast over me, saying, my own hand has saved me. God is not arranging a victory here; he is arranging an account of the victory that nobody can misread. The reduction is a piece of theology carried out with manpower.

'"Now therefore proclaim in the ears of the people, saying, 'Whoever is fearful and trembling, let him return home.'" Then 22,000 of the people returned, and 10,000 remained.'

The first cut is not Gideon's invention. Moses had written the rule into Israel's law of war: before a battle the officers shall say, is there any man who is fearful and fainthearted? Let him go back to his house, lest he make the heart of his fellows melt like his own (Deut. 20:8).

Gideon reads out the standing statute, and two thirds of his army goes home. Twenty-two thousand men admit in public that they are afraid and walk away, which tells you what the seven years had done to the country.

'And the LORD said to Gideon, "The people are still too many."'

Ten thousand against a valley full of camels, and the sentence comes again.

'"Every one who laps the water with his tongue, as a dog laps, you shall set by himself. Likewise, every one who kneels down to drink." And the number of those who lapped, putting their hands to their mouths, was 300 men, but all the rest of the people knelt down to drink water.'

Then the test at the water, and the temptation to make it clever should be resisted.

A great deal has been written about the alertness of men who scoop water to the mouth and keep their eyes up, as against those who put their faces down to drink. It may be right. The text does not say so, and it does not say the three hundred were chosen for a quality at all.

What the text says is that God sorted them by something arbitrary and kept the smaller group. The point of a test that selects three hundred out of ten thousand is the three hundred. If the lappers had been the alert ones, we would be back at a victory that could be credited to good selection, and verse 2 has already ruled that out.

'So the people took provisions in their hands, and their trumpets. And he sent all the rest of Israel every man to his tent, but retained the 300 men.'

The men who leave hand over their supplies and their trumpets. That detail is quietly important: three hundred men are about to be issued with an army's worth of trumpets, and the plan in verse 16 depends on it.

Ninety-nine per cent of the army has gone home, and Gideon is standing on a hillside above a valley full of Midianites with a small company, a great many horns, and a promise.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: That night God tells him to go down, because I have given it into your hand (v. 9) — and then adds a clause no one expects: but if you are afraid to go down, go down to the camp with Purah your servant (v. 10). He goes, with Purah, to the edge of the enemy outposts (v. 11), where the raiders lie along the valley like locusts with camels beyond counting (v. 12). And he overhears a man telling a dream about a barley loaf rolling into the camp and flattening a tent, and his comrade interpreting it as the sword of Gideon (vv. 13-14). Gideon worships on the spot and goes back to raise the three hundred (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: God's answer to the fear is not a rebuke. He offers the frightened man a companion for the walk and a piece of information to bring back, and lets him decide whether he needs them.
verseByVerse.examples: A barley loaf is peasant food, the bread of the poor and the cheapest grain in the country — and barley is what the Midianites had been stealing every harvest for seven years. In the dream it is what knocks the tent flat. Even the enemy's nightmares know who is small in this story.

verseByVerse.quote: That same night the LORD said to him, "Arise, go down against the camp, for I have given it into your hand. But if you are afraid to go down, go down to the camp with Purah your servant. And you shall hear what they say, and afterward your hands shall be strengthened to go down against the camp." Then he went down with Purah his servant to the outposts of the armed men who were in the camp. And the Midianites and the Amalekites and all the people of the East lay along the valley like locusts in abundance, and their camels were without number, as the sand that is on the seashore in abundance. When Gideon came, behold, a man was telling a dream to his comrade. And he said, "Behold, I dreamed a dream, and behold, a cake of barley bread tumbled into the camp of Midian and came to the tent and struck it so that it fell and turned it upside down, so that the tent lay flat." And his comrade answered, "This is no other than the sword of Gideon the son of Joash, a man of Israel; God has given into his hand Midian and all the camp." As soon as Gideon heard the telling of the dream and its interpretation, he worshiped. And he returned to the camp of Israel and said, "Arise, for the LORD has given the host of Midian into your hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'That same night the LORD said to him, "Arise, go down against the camp, for I have given it into your hand. But if you are afraid to go down, go down to the camp with Purah your servant."'

Two sentences, and the second is one of the most humane things God says in the Old Testament.

The first is the order and the promise, in the usual form: go down, for I have given it into your hand. The second is God adding, unprompted, a provision for the state he knows this man is in.

But if you are afraid to go down — and note what does not follow. Not do not be afraid. Not a rebuke for still being frightened after the angel, the fire, the Spirit and two nights of fleeces. God simply grants the fear and works with it: take Purah with you, and go and listen.

Nobody tells Gideon he ought not to need this. He is given a companion for the walk and told what he will find when he gets there: afterward your hands shall be strengthened.

God is not embarrassed by his servant's nerves and does not require him to pretend. He gives him a plan for them.

'Then he went down with Purah his servant to the outposts of the armed men who were in the camp. And the Midianites and the Amalekites and all the people of the East lay along the valley like locusts in abundance, and their camels were without number, as the sand that is on the seashore in abundance.'

He takes the servant. The offer was conditional and Gideon accepts it, and the narrator lets that stand without comment.

What he sees when he gets down there is not reassuring. The valley is full: locusts again, and camels beyond counting, and the phrase used for them is the one God used to Abraham about his own descendants — as the sand that is on the seashore.

'When Gideon came, behold, a man was telling a dream to his comrade. And he said, "Behold, I dreamed a dream, and behold, a cake of barley bread tumbled into the camp of Midian and came to the tent and struck it so that it fell and turned it upside down, so that the tent lay flat."'

He arrives at the exact moment a man is describing a dream, and the dream is about bread.

A cake of barley bread. Barley is the cheap grain, the bread of the poor, what you eat when you cannot afford wheat — and barley is precisely what these men have been stealing off Israelite threshing floors for seven years. In the dream, a loaf of the stuff they have been robbing rolls into the camp and knocks a tent flat.

'And his comrade answered, "This is no other than the sword of Gideon the son of Joash, a man of Israel; God has given into his hand Midian and all the camp."'

The second man interprets it, and gets it exactly right, including the name.

Two enemy soldiers, in the dark, in their own camp, telling each other that God has handed them over to a farmer from Ophrah. The one sentence Gideon needed to hear is spoken by the enemy, in the enemy's language, about the enemy's own destruction.

'As soon as Gideon heard the telling of the dream and its interpretation, he worshiped.'

He worships. Standing in the dark at the edge of a hostile camp with one servant beside him, the first thing he does is bow.

See what it took. Not the angel, not the fire, not the Spirit, not the fleece: a frightened man overhearing a stranger's nightmare. God knew what would work on Gideon and had it waiting for him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Three hundred men are divided into three companies, and each man is given a trumpet and an empty jar with a torch inside it (v. 16). The instructions are simple: watch me, and do what I do (v. 17). At the beginning of the middle watch, just after the guard changes, they blow the trumpets and smash the jars (vv. 18-19). Torches in the left hand, trumpets in the right, and a shout — a sword for the LORD and for Gideon (v. 20). Then verse 21: every man stood in his place around the camp, and the whole army ran. And the LORD set every man's sword against his comrade (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: Nobody in the three hundred has a hand free for a weapon. A torch in one hand and a trumpet in the other is the whole equipment, and the writer makes a point of saying so. They stood still and made a noise, and the enemy destroyed itself in the dark.
verseByVerse.examples: The battle plan is a piece of theatre.
