Three hundred trumpets in the night sound like three hundred companies, because a trumpet belonged to a unit commander; three hundred torches appearing at once look like an army that has already surrounded the camp. The Midianites are not defeated by the three hundred. They are defeated by what they concluded about them.

verseByVerse.quote: And he divided the 300 men into three companies and put trumpets into the hands of all of them and empty jars, with torches inside the jars. And he said to them, "Look at me, and do likewise. When I come to the outskirts of the camp, do as I do. When I blow the trumpet, I and all who are with me, then blow the trumpets also on every side of all the camp and shout, 'For the LORD and for Gideon.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And he divided the 300 men into three companies and put trumpets into the hands of all of them and empty jars, with torches inside the jars.'

Now the equipment, and it repays counting on the fingers.

Each man gets a trumpet. Each man gets an empty jar. Inside each jar, a lit torch, which is what the jar is for — a clay pot over a flame hides it completely until the pot is broken.

That is two hands, and there is nothing in either of them that can hurt anybody. No sword is issued to the three hundred. The men are going into a night attack on a valley full of raiders carrying a musical instrument and a pot.

'And he said to them, "Look at me, and do likewise. When I come to the outskirts of the camp, do as I do. When I blow the trumpet, I and all who are with me, then blow the trumpets also on every side of all the camp and shout, 'For the LORD and for Gideon.'"'

The whole battle order is four words long: look at me, and do likewise.

There is no strategy to memorise and no contingency. Three companies take up positions on three sides of a sleeping army in the dark, and every man watches one man on a hillside and copies him.

Hear the shout as it stands, because it names the arrangement exactly: for the LORD and for Gideon. Not for Israel, not for the tribes, and not for freedom. A God and a farmer, in that order.

verseByVerse.quote: So Gideon and the hundred men who were with him came to the outskirts of the camp at the beginning of the middle watch, when they had just set the watch. And they blew the trumpets and smashed the jars that were in their hands. Then the three companies blew the trumpets and broke the jars. They held in their left hands the torches, and in their right hands the trumpets to blow. And they cried out, "A sword for the LORD and for Gideon!" Every man stood in his place around the camp, and all the army ran. They cried out and fled. When they blew the 300 trumpets, the LORD set every man's sword against his comrade and against all the army. And the army fled as far as Beth-shittah toward Zererah, as far as the border of Abel-meholah, by Tabbath.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'So Gideon and the hundred men who were with him came to the outskirts of the camp at the beginning of the middle watch, when they had just set the watch. And they blew the trumpets and smashed the jars that were in their hands.'

The timing is professional. The middle watch begins around ten at night, and Gideon moves at the changeover — the moment when the new sentries are settling in, their eyes are not yet adjusted, and the men coming off duty are heading for their blankets.

Then three hundred trumpets, and three hundred clay pots smashed at once.

'Then the three companies blew the trumpets and broke the jars. They held in their left hands the torches, and in their right hands the trumpets to blow. And they cried out, "A sword for the LORD and for Gideon!"'

The writer takes the trouble to tell us what is in each hand, and the arithmetic of it is the point: torches on the left, trumpets on the right, and no third hand for the sword they are shouting about.

Consider what this looks like from inside the camp. A man wakes in the dark to trumpets on three sides at once — and in that world a trumpet belonged to the commander of a unit, so three hundred horns means three hundred companies. At the same instant, three hundred flames appear in a ring where a moment ago there was nothing. And a war cry announcing a sword.

Nobody in that valley sees three hundred men. Everybody in it hears an army that has already surrounded them.

'Every man stood in his place around the camp, and all the army ran. They cried out and fled.'

Verse 21 is the sentence to hold on to. Every man stood in his place around the camp. The three hundred do not charge, do not advance, do not engage. They stand still, holding a light and making a noise, and the enemy disintegrates in front of them.

'When they blew the 300 trumpets, the LORD set every man's sword against his comrade and against all the army.'

Here is what actually killed the Midianites: each other, in the dark, in a panic, unable to tell friend from enemy.

The subject of the verb is God. The LORD set every man's sword against his comrade. Verse 2 said the army had to be small enough that Israel could not claim the credit, and the final arrangement removes even the sword. Three hundred men with pots and horns stood still, and the enemy destroyed itself.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now the tribes are called out — Naphtali, Asher and all Manasseh — and they pursue (v. 23). Gideon sends to Ephraim to seize the water crossings as far as the Jordan, cutting the retreat (v. 24). Two princes of Midian are taken and killed at places that keep their names, the rock of Oreb and the winepress of Zeeb, and their heads are brought to Gideon across the Jordan (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology: The men who were sent home get the pursuit. The three hundred did the part that could only be credited to God, and the rest of Israel does the ordinary work of finishing a rout — which is real work, and is not despised.
verseByVerse.examples: Zeeb dies at a winepress. Gideon met the angel of the LORD threshing wheat in one, hiding from these very people. The book does not comment on it and does not need to.

verseByVerse.quote: And the men of Israel were called out from Naphtali and from Asher and from all Manasseh, and they pursued after Midian. Gideon sent messengers throughout all the hill country of Ephraim, saying, "Come down against the Midianites and capture the waters against them, as far as Beth-barah, and also the Jordan." So all the men of Ephraim were called out, and they captured the waters as far as Beth-barah, and also the Jordan. And they captured the two princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb. They killed Oreb at the rock of Oreb, and Zeeb they killed at the winepress of Zeeb. Then they pursued Midian, and they brought the heads of Oreb and Zeeb to Gideon across the Jordan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And the men of Israel were called out from Naphtali and from Asher and from all Manasseh, and they pursued after Midian.'

Now the rest of Israel is recalled — including, presumably, a good many of the twenty-two thousand who had gone home admitting they were afraid.

There is something generous in the arrangement. The part of the work that could only ever be credited to God was done by three hundred men holding crockery. The pursuit, which is ordinary soldiering and takes days, is given back to the tribes.

God arranged an unmistakable miracle and then handed the follow-up to normal people doing normal work, and the second half is not despised in the telling.

'Gideon sent messengers throughout all the hill country of Ephraim, saying, "Come down against the Midianites and capture the waters against them, as far as Beth-barah, and also the Jordan."'

Gideon's own generalship is sound. He sends to Ephraim to seize the fords before the fleeing army reaches them, exactly as Ehud had done at the same river, and the retreat is closed.

'And they captured the two princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb. They killed Oreb at the rock of Oreb, and Zeeb they killed at the winepress of Zeeb.'

Two enemy princes are taken and killed, and the places keep their names afterwards, which is how a country remembers a night like this.

The second location is worth a moment. Zeeb dies at a winepress.

The last winepress in this story had a young man crouched in it, threshing wheat where the wind could not reach, hiding a few bushels from the very people this prince commanded. The Midianites are now dying in one.

The book makes nothing of it, and there is nothing to make. God took a man out of a pit, gave him back his own name as a nickname daring a dead god to answer, reduced his army by ninety-nine per cent so that nobody could get the story wrong, sent him to overhear a stranger's dream about a barley loaf, and had him stand still in the dark holding a jar while the valley emptied.

Isaiah, seven hundred years later, was still using this night as shorthand for what God does to an oppressor: the rod of his oppressor you have broken as on the day of Midian (Isa. 9:4) — and the verses on either side of it are about a light shining on people who walked in darkness, and a child who is born.

7.theology:
An explanation, not just a victory. Verse 2 gives the reason for every reduction that follows, and it is theological rather than military. God will not win this in a way that leaves room for my own hand has saved me. The arithmetic runs from thirty-two thousand to three hundred to a battle in which nobody on Israel's side draws a sword at all.

God works with the fear rather than against it. The offer in verse 10 is unprompted and conditional: if you are afraid, take Purah. There is no rebuke in it and no requirement to pretend. Gideon accepts, goes down, hears what he needs and worships in the dark. What finally strengthened him was not another sign from heaven but a stranger's nightmare, and God had it waiting.

Standing still. The three hundred hold a torch in the left hand and a trumpet in the right, and verse 21 says every man stood in his place around the camp. They do not charge. The enemy is destroyed by what it concludes in the dark, and the writer names the agent: the LORD set every man's sword against his comrade.

The night of Midian. Seven centuries later Isaiah is still using this as the standard picture of God breaking an oppressor — the rod of his oppressor you have broken as on the day of Midian (Isa. 9:4) — and the verses around it are about light shining on people who walked in darkness, and a child who is born to us.
7.examples:
Then: An army of thirty-two thousand was cut to three hundred on purpose, and the three hundred were sent into a night attack carrying a pot and a horn. They stood still in a ring around a sleeping valley, broke the pots, and watched an army kill itself in the dark.

Now: Verse 10 is the one to keep. Notice what God does with a frightened man who has already been given more assurance than most people get in a lifetime: he does not shame him, does not withdraw the commission, and does not tell him to feel differently. He offers him a companion for the walk down. If you are waiting to stop being afraid before you go, this is a chapter about a man who went with somebody else beside him.

8.title: Gideon's Failure
8.text: <sup>1</sup>Then the men of Ephraim said to him, "What is this that you have done to us, not to call us when you went to fight against Midian?" And they accused him fiercely.<sup>2</sup>And he said to them, "What have I done now in comparison with you? Is not the gleaning of the grapes of Ephraim better than the grape harvest of Abiezer?<sup>3</sup>God has given into your hands the princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb. What have I been able to do in comparison with you?" Then their anger against him subsided when he said this.<sup>4</sup>And Gideon came to the Jordan and crossed over, he and the 300 men who were with him, exhausted yet pursuing.<sup>5</sup>So he said to the men of Succoth, "Please give loaves of bread to the people who follow me, for they are exhausted, and I am pursuing after Zebah and Zalmunna, the kings of Midian."<sup>6</sup>And the officials of Succoth said, "Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your hand, that we should give bread to your army?"<sup>7</sup>So Gideon said, "Well then, when the LORD has given Zebah and Zalmunna into my hand, I will flail your flesh with the thorns of the wilderness and with briers."<sup>8</sup>And from there he went up to Penuel, and spoke to them in the same way, and the men of Penuel answered him as the men of Succoth had answered.<sup>9</sup>And he said to the men of Penuel, "When I come again in peace, I will break down this tower."<sup>10</sup>Now Zebah and Zalmunna were in Karkor with their army, about 15,000 men, all who were left of all the army of the people of the East, for there had fallen 120,000 men who drew the sword.<sup>11</sup>And Gideon went up by the way of the tent dwellers east of Nobah and Jogbehah and attacked the army, for the army felt secure.<sup>12</sup>And Zebah and Zalmunna fled, and he pursued them and captured the two kings of Midian, Zebah and Zalmunna, and he threw all the army into a panic.<sup>13</sup>Then Gideon the son of Joash returned from the battle by the ascent of Heres.<sup>14</sup>And he captured a young man of Succoth and questioned him. And he wrote down for him the officials and elders of Succoth, seventy-seven men.<sup>15</sup>And he came to the men of Succoth and said, "Behold Zebah and Zalmunna, about whom you taunted me, saying, 'Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your hand, that we should give bread to your men who are exhausted?'"<sup>16</sup>And he took the elders of the city, and he took thorns of the wilderness and briers and with them taught the men of Succoth a lesson.<sup>17</sup>And he broke down the tower of Penuel and killed the men of the city.<sup>18</sup>Then he said to Zebah and Zalmunna, "Where are the men whom you killed at Tabor?" They answered, "As you are, so were they. Every one of them resembled the son of a king."<sup>19</sup>And he said, "They were my brothers, the sons of my mother. As the LORD lives, if you had saved them alive, I would not kill you."<sup>20</sup>So he said to Jether his firstborn, "Rise and kill them!" But the young man did not draw his sword, for he was afraid, because he was still a young man.<sup>21</sup>Then Zebah and Zalmunna said, "Rise yourself and fall upon us, for as the man is, so is his strength." And Gideon arose and killed Zebah and Zalmunna, and he took the crescent ornaments that were on the necks of their camels.<sup>22</sup>Then the men of Israel said to Gideon, "Rule over us, you and your son and your grandson also, for you have saved us from the hand of Midian."<sup>23</sup>Gideon said to them, "I will not rule over you, and my son will not rule over you; the LORD will rule over you."<sup>24</sup>And Gideon said to them, "Let me make a request of you: every one of you give me the earrings from his spoil." (For they had golden earrings, because they were Ishmaelites.)<sup>25</sup>And they answered, "We will willingly give them." And they spread a cloak, and every man threw in it the earrings of his spoil.<sup>26</sup>And the weight of the golden earrings that he requested was 1,700 shekels of gold, besides the crescent ornaments and the pendants and the purple garments worn by the kings of Midian, and besides the collars that were around the necks of their camels.<sup>27</sup>And Gideon made an ephod of it and put it in his city, in Ophrah. And all Israel whored after it there, and it became a snare to Gideon and to his family.<sup>28</sup>So Midian was subdued before the people of Israel, and they raised their heads no more. And the land had rest for forty years in the days of Gideon.<sup>29</sup>Jerubbaal the son of Joash went and lived in his own house.<sup>30</sup>Now Gideon had seventy sons, his own offspring, for he had many wives.<sup>31</sup>And his concubine who was in Shechem also bore him a son, and he called his name Abimelech.<sup>32</sup>And Gideon the son of Joash died in a good old age and was buried in the tomb of Joash his father, at Ophrah of the Abiezrites.<sup>33</sup>As soon as Gideon died, the people of Israel turned again and whored after the Baals and made Baal-berith their god.<sup>34</sup>And the people of Israel did not remember the LORD their God, who had delivered them from the hand of all their enemies on every side,<sup>35</sup>and they did not show steadfast love to the family of Jerubbaal (that is, Gideon) in return for all the good that he had done to Israel.
8.overview:
Chapter 8 is the tragic underside of Gideon's story, the slow corruption of a deliverer. The man who tore down Baal's altar and routed Midian with three hundred now begins a downward drift that ends in idolatry and family disaster. The chapter opens with the proud Ephraimites quarreling over not being called to the battle sooner; Gideon soothes them with a diplomatic answer. But as he pursues the Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna across the Jordan, a harder edge appears.

The towns of Succoth and Penuel refuse Gideon's exhausted men bread, doubting he will win. Gideon's response is vengeful and disproportionate — he threatens them, and on his return he flays the elders of Succoth with thorns and tears down the tower of Penuel, killing its men. The deliverer is becoming a tyrant. He captures and personally executes Zebah and Zalmunna, partly in blood-vengeance for his own brothers they had killed.

Then comes the chapter's great moment of apparent humility. Israel offers Gideon the crown — 'Rule over us, you and your son and your grandson.' Gideon refuses with seemingly perfect theology: 'I will not rule over you... the LORD will rule over you.' But in the very next breath he asks for the golden earrings of the plunder, fashions them into an ephod, and sets it up in his city. 'All Israel whored after it there, and it became a snare to Gideon and to his family.' The man who destroyed one idol erects another. He refuses the crown but takes the wealth and the worship; he declines to be king in name while behaving like one — naming a son Abimelech, 'my father is king.'

Here is the sobering theology of the chapter: the deliverer himself becomes the snare. Gideon's tragedy is the tragedy of every human savior — even the Spirit-clothed, idol-breaking hero finishes flawed, drawing the worship to himself and leaving a legacy of apostasy. Israel does not need a better Gideon; Israel needs a Deliverer who will not fail in the end, who will not turn the people's gratitude into idolatry, who when offered every kingdom will worship God alone. Gideon's golden ephod cries out for the King who is himself without sin.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Ephraimites angrily confront Gideon for not summoning them earlier to the battle. Gideon defuses them with a soft, flattering answer.
verseByVerse.theology: A soft answer turns away wrath. Yet Ephraim's wounded pride foreshadows the tribal jealousy that will tear Israel apart.
verseByVerse.examples: Gentleness can disarm conflict. But the craving for recognition, even in God's work, is a root of bitter division.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the men of Ephraim said to him, "What is this that you have done to us, not to call us when you went to fight against Midian?" And they accused him fiercely. And he said to them, "What have I done now in comparison with you? Is not the gleaning of the grapes of Ephraim better than the vintage of Abiezer?" ...Then their anger against him subsided.
verseByVerse.commentary: Hardly has the victory been won when the Ephraimites pick a quarrel. 'What is this that you have done to us, not to call us...?' They are not angry that Midian oppressed Israel; they are angry that they missed the glory. Wounded tribal pride, not zeal for God, drives their fierce accusation. Gideon responds with remarkable diplomacy, a soft answer that magnifies them and minimizes himself: 'Is not the gleaning of the grapes of Ephraim' — your capture of Oreb and Zeeb — 'better than the vintage of Abiezer?' — my whole campaign? He gives them the credit, and their anger subsides. Davis credits the wisdom of the answer; 'a soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger' (Prov. 15:1), and Gideon proves it. Yet there is a darker undertone. Ephraim's touchiness about honor is a symptom of the tribal jealousy that will eventually tear Israel apart — indeed, Jephthah will face the same Ephraimite pride in chapter 12 and answer it not with soft words but with civil war and the slaughter at the fords. The craving for recognition, even in the work of God, is a poison. How often ministry is wounded not by enemies without but by the bruised egos within, by those more concerned to be called than to see God glorified. Gideon's gentleness is admirable; Ephraim's pride is a warning. (cf. Prov. 15:1; Phil. 2:3)

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–9 — Succoth and Penuel Refuse Aid
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Pursuing the Midianite kings, Gideon's exhausted men ask Succoth and Penuel for bread. Both towns refuse, doubting his victory. Gideon vows vengeance on them.
verseByVerse.theology: The towns' refusal exposes a failure of faith and solidarity within Israel itself. Gideon's vow of vengeance shows his own hardening heart.
verseByVerse.examples: Cynical refusal to help God's work when the outcome looks uncertain is its own kind of unbelief. Yet vengeance is not ours to take.

verseByVerse.quote: And Gideon came to the Jordan and crossed over, he and the 300 men with him, exhausted yet pursuing. So he said to the men of Succoth, "Please give loaves of bread to the people who follow me..." And the officials of Succoth said, "Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your hand...?" ...he said, "Well then, when the LORD has given Zebah and Zalmunna into my hand, I will flail your flesh with the thorns..."
verseByVerse.commentary: The three hundred are 'exhausted yet pursuing' — a phrase that captures the dogged faith of those who press on past their strength. Gideon asks the Israelite towns of Succoth and Penuel for bread, a reasonable request from kinsmen to weary soldiers fighting their common enemy. But both towns sneer and refuse: 'Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your hand?' In other words, you have not won yet; why should we risk Midianite reprisal by helping a man who may lose? Their refusal is unbelief and self-interest dressed as prudence. They will not commit until they see the victory secured. Davis notes the cynicism: they hedge their bets, declining to aid God's deliverer until success is guaranteed. There is a rebuke here for the faith that will only help God's work once it looks like a sure thing. But Gideon's reaction is no better. Instead of grieving their unbelief, he swells with vengeful fury, vowing to flail the elders of Succoth with thorns and tear down the tower of Penuel. The diplomat of verse 2 has become the avenger of verse 7. The narrator is charting Gideon's hardening; the meek man who hid in the winepress now threatens his own people with torture. Success, it seems, has begun to corrupt him. Vengeance belongs to the Lord, not to us (Rom. 12:19), but Gideon has begun to take it into his own hands. (cf. Rom. 12:19; 1 Sam. 25:21–22)

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–17 — The Capture of the Kings and Vengeance
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Gideon defeats the remaining Midianite host and captures Zebah and Zalmunna. Returning, he makes good his threats — punishing the elders of Succoth with thorns and destroying the tower of Penuel, killing its men.
verseByVerse.theology: God grants the full victory, but Gideon's brutal reprisals against Israelite towns reveal a deliverer increasingly driven by personal vengeance rather than zeal for God.
verseByVerse.examples: The line between righteous justice and personal vengeance is easily crossed. Power and success can harden even a once-humble heart.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Zebah and Zalmunna were in Karkor with their army... So Gideon... captured the two kings of Midian, Zebah and Zalmunna, and he threw all the army into a panic. ...he took the elders of the city, and he took thorns of the wilderness and briers and with them taught the men of Succoth a lesson. And he broke down the tower of Penuel and killed the men of the city.
verseByVerse.commentary: Gideon completes the military victory, surprising the remnant of the Midianite army at Karkor and capturing the two kings Zebah and Zalmunna. God has given him everything he asked — the kings are in his hand, exactly as he had vowed. But the use he makes of his triumph is troubling. He carries out his threats against his own people: the elders of Succoth are punished with thorns and briers, and the tower of Penuel is torn down and its men killed. Davis observes the sobering trajectory — Gideon now wages war against Israelite towns with the same ferocity he showed against Midian. Whatever the towns deserved for their cynical refusal, the punishment is disproportionate and personal; the men of Penuel are killed, not merely rebuked. The Spirit-clothed deliverer is slipping into the role of the vengeful warlord. There is a hard lesson here about the corrupting power of success. The same man who trembled in a winepress, who needed two fleeces and a midnight reconnaissance to believe God, now strides through the land settling scores with thorns and the sword. Victory has not sanctified him; it has emboldened his flesh. Power tests the heart as adversity never could. Gideon passed the test of weakness magnificently; he is failing the test of strength. The crown he will soon refuse he is already, in spirit, beginning to wear. (cf. Prov. 16:32; Deut. 32:35)

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to Zebah and Zalmunna, "Where are the men whom you killed at Tabor?" They answered, "...they were like you, every one of them resembling the son of a king." And he said, "They were my brothers, the sons of my mother..." ...So Gideon arose and killed Zebah and Zalmunna...
verseByVerse.commentary: The interrogation of the captured kings reveals a personal motive beneath Gideon's pursuit. The men they killed at Tabor were Gideon's own brothers, 'the sons of my mother.' This was blood-vengeance as much as national deliverance; Gideon hunted these kings partly to avenge his family. He commands his young son Jether to execute them — an attempt to confer the honor of the kill on his heir, another hint of the dynastic ambition stirring in him — but the boy is too afraid. So Gideon does it himself. The kings die with a grim dignity, even noting that the slain brothers 'resembled the son of a king' — and the reader catches the irony, for Gideon's family carried itself with royal bearing. Davis notes how the personal and the public have become tangled in Gideon; the LORD's battle and Gideon's vendetta are no longer cleanly distinguishable. The deliverance that began as pure grace — God saving a helpless people through a fearful nobody — has acquired the stains of personal grievance and family pride. This is the perennial danger for every servant of God: that the Lord's work and our own agendas blur together until we can no longer tell whether we fight for his glory or our own. The honor Gideon tried to give his son foreshadows the dynastic disaster of Abimelech in chapter 9. (cf. Num. 35:19; Jer. 17:9)

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel offers Gideon a hereditary monarchy for delivering them. Gideon refuses with seemingly perfect theology: 'The LORD will rule over you.'
verseByVerse.theology: Gideon's words confess the great truth that the LORD alone is Israel's true King. Yet his subsequent actions betray a dynastic ambition his words deny.
verseByVerse.examples: It is possible to confess the right theology with our lips while contradicting it with our lives. The LORD alone is King.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the men of Israel said to Gideon, "Rule over us, you and your son and your grandson also, for you have saved us from the hand of Midian." Gideon said to them, "I will not rule over you, and my son will not rule over you; the LORD will rule over you."
verseByVerse.commentary: Israel offers Gideon a hereditary throne — 'you and your son and your grandson' — and on its face Gideon's refusal is magnificent theology: 'I will not rule over you, and my son will not rule over you; the LORD will rule over you.' This is the very heart of Israel's covenant ideal. Yahweh is Israel's true King; for a man to claim the throne is to usurp the kingship of God. Gideon's words echo the right order of things, the theocratic conviction that would make Israel uneasy about monarchy right up to Samuel's day. If Gideon had only meant it, the chapter might have ended in glory. But the tragedy of the next verses is that his deeds will betray his creed. Davis catches the painful gap: Gideon says the King is the LORD, and then proceeds to take royal plunder, set up a royal shrine, accumulate a royal household of wives and concubines, and name a son Abimelech, 'my father is king.' He declines the title while grasping the substance. Here is one of Scripture's most searching warnings: it is entirely possible to confess sound theology with the mouth while denying it with the life. The right words about God's kingship are no proof of submission to it. Gideon's lips crown the LORD; Gideon's life reaches for the crown himself. The orthodoxy of the tongue must be matched by the obedience of the heart, or it becomes a cloak for idolatry. (cf. 1 Sam. 8:7; Matt. 7:21)

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Gideon asks for the golden earrings of the plunder, fashions them into an ephod, and sets it up in Ophrah. All Israel 'whored after it,' and it became a snare to Gideon and his family.
verseByVerse.theology: The man who tore down one idol erects another. The deliverer himself becomes the snare — the tragic flaw of every human savior.
verseByVerse.examples: Even good things — even religious objects — become idols when they draw worship to themselves. The savior who becomes the snare cries out for the sinless King.

verseByVerse.quote: And Gideon said to them, "Let me make a request of you: every one of you give me the earrings from his spoil." ...And Gideon made an ephod of it and put it in his city, in Ophrah. And all Israel whored after it there, and it became a snare to Gideon and to his family.
verseByVerse.commentary: In the very breath after refusing the crown, Gideon makes a request that unravels his confession. He asks for the golden earrings of the plunder — a staggering weight of gold — and fashions them into an 'ephod.' Whatever its exact form, perhaps a richly ornamented priestly garment or cult object, Gideon sets it up in his own city of Ophrah, establishing a rival center of worship apart from the tabernacle. And the result is catastrophic: 'all Israel whored after it there, and it became a snare to Gideon and to his family.' The verb 'whored' is the language of spiritual adultery used throughout the book for idolatry; the very word once applied to Baal worship now describes Israel's devotion to Gideon's ephod. The unbearable irony, which Davis drives home, is that the man who began by tearing down the altar of Baal ends by erecting a snare of his own — and the man named Jerubbaal, 'let Baal contend,' becomes the source of fresh idolatry. The ephod was probably intended as a memorial to God's victory, even an instrument of worship; but good intentions could not keep it from becoming an idol. This is the deepest tragedy of the chapter and a parable of every human deliverer: the savior himself becomes the snare. Even the gold dedicated to God, even the religious object, even the memorial of grace, will be 'whored after' by the idolatrous heart. Only a Savior who is himself sinless can refuse every crown of self-glory and lead his people to worship God alone. (cf. Exod. 32:2–4; 1 Cor. 10:14)

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–35 — Gideon's Death and Israel's Relapse
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The land has rest forty years. Gideon lives like a king with many wives and seventy sons, and names a son by his Shechemite concubine 'Abimelech.' When Gideon dies, Israel immediately whores after Baal again and forgets both the LORD and Gideon's house.
verseByVerse.theology: The cycle repeats: the moment the deliverer dies, Israel relapses. Gideon's royal household and the ominous name Abimelech set the stage for the horror of chapter 9.
verseByVerse.examples: Human deliverance always wears off at the deliverer's death. Ingratitude toward God and his servants is the dark fruit of the unconverted heart.

verseByVerse.quote: So Midian was subdued before the people of Israel... And the land had rest forty years in the days of Gideon. ...Now Gideon had seventy sons, his own offspring... and his concubine who was in Shechem also bore him a son, and he called his name Abimelech. ...As soon as Gideon died, the people of Israel turned again and whored after the Baals...
verseByVerse.commentary: The chapter closes with the familiar rhythm of the cycle and a heavy sense of foreboding. Midian is subdued, and the land has rest forty years — a generation of peace, the fruit of God's deliverance. But the narrator's portrait of Gideon's later life is unmistakably royal: he takes 'many wives' and fathers 'seventy sons' — a harem and a dynasty, the marks of an oriental king. He has refused the title but lives the role. Most ominous is the son born to his Shechemite concubine, whom he names Abimelech — 'my father is king.' The name betrays what Gideon's confession denied; whatever his lips said about the LORD ruling, his heart was royal, and his son's very name proclaims it. This name will become the title of chapter 9's nightmare. Then the cycle turns with brutal speed: 'As soon as Gideon died, the people of Israel turned again and whored after the Baals.' The deliverance lasted exactly as long as the deliverer lived. They forgot the LORD their God who had delivered them, and they showed no kindness to Gideon's house. Davis notes the double ingratitude — toward God and toward his servant — that marks the depraved heart. Once more the book's great cry rises: the deliverer dies, and all is undone. Israel needs the King whose death is not the end but the very means of salvation, whose rising secures a rest that no relapse can destroy. (cf. Judg. 2:19; Ps. 106:13)

8.theology:
The Corruption of Success. The fearful man of the winepress, once tested by weakness, fails the test of strength. Victory hardens Gideon into a vengeful avenger and an aspiring king. Power tries the heart as adversity never could; success is the more dangerous trial.

The Deliverer Becomes the Snare. The man who tore down Baal's altar erects the golden ephod, and 'all Israel whored after it' (v. 27). Every human savior finishes flawed, drawing worship to himself. This is the book's argument that Israel needs not a better Gideon but a sinless King.

Orthodox Lips, Idolatrous Life. Gideon confesses 'the LORD will rule over you' (v. 23) and then lives like a king, naming his son 'my father is king.' Sound theology on the tongue can mask rebellion in the heart. Not those who say but those who do the Father's will (Matt. 7:21).
8.examples:
Then: The hero who broke Baal's altar and routed Midian with three hundred ended his days taking vengeance on his own people, refusing the crown with his lips while grasping its substance, and erecting a golden ephod that snared all Israel into idolatry — and the moment he died, Israel relapsed.

Now: Beware the test of success more than the test of hardship; many who stood in weakness fall in strength. Beware the idols we make even of good and religious things, which draw to themselves the worship due to God alone. And beware the orthodox confession that the life contradicts. Look away from every Gideon to the sinless King who, offered all the kingdoms, worshiped God alone.

9.title: Abimelech the Bramble King
9.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Abimelech the son of Jerubbaal went to Shechem to his mother's relatives and said to them and to the whole clan of his mother's family,<sup>2</sup>"Say in the ears of all the leaders of Shechem, 'Which is better for you, that all seventy of the sons of Jerubbaal rule over you, or that one rule over you?' Remember also that I am your bone and your flesh."<sup>3</sup>And his mother's relatives spoke all these words on his behalf in the ears of all the leaders of Shechem, and their hearts inclined to follow Abimelech, for they said, "He is our brother."<sup>4</sup>And they gave him seventy pieces of silver out of the house of Baal-berith with which Abimelech hired worthless and reckless fellows, who followed him.<sup>5</sup>And he went to his father's house at Ophrah and killed his brothers the sons of Jerubbaal, seventy men, on one stone. But Jotham the youngest son of Jerubbaal was left, for he hid himself.<sup>6</sup>And all the leaders of Shechem came together, and all Beth-millo, and they went and made Abimelech king, by the oak of the pillar at Shechem.<sup>7</sup>When it was told to Jotham, he went and stood on top of Mount Gerizim and cried aloud and said to them, "Listen to me, you leaders of Shechem, that God may listen to you.<sup>8</sup>The trees once went out to anoint a king over them, and they said to the olive tree, 'Reign over us.'<sup>9</sup>But the olive tree said to them, 'Shall I leave my abundance, by which gods and men are honored, and go hold sway over the trees?'<sup>10</sup>And the trees said to the fig tree, 'You come and reign over us.'<sup>11</sup>But the fig tree said to them, 'Shall I leave my sweetness and my good fruit and go hold sway over the trees?'<sup>12</sup>And the trees said to the vine, 'You come and reign over us.'<sup>13</sup>But the vine said to them, 'Shall I leave my wine that cheers God and men and go hold sway over the trees?'<sup>14</sup>Then all the trees said to the bramble, 'You come and reign over us.'<sup>15</sup>And the bramble said to the trees, 'If in good faith you are anointing me king over you, then come and take refuge in my shade, but if not, let fire come out of the bramble and devour the cedars of Lebanon.'<sup>16</sup>"Now therefore, if you acted in good faith and integrity when you made Abimelech king, and if you have dealt well with Jerubbaal and his house and have done to him as his deeds deserved—<sup>17</sup>for my father fought for you and risked his life and delivered you from the hand of Midian,<sup>18</sup>and you have risen up against my father's house this day and have killed his sons, seventy men on one stone, and have made Abimelech, the son of his female servant, king over the leaders of Shechem, because he is your relative—<sup>19</sup>if you then have acted in good faith and integrity with Jerubbaal and with his house this day, then rejoice in Abimelech, and let him also rejoice in you.<sup>20</sup>But if not, let fire come out from Abimelech and devour the leaders of Shechem and Beth-millo; and let fire come out from the leaders of Shechem and from Beth-millo and devour Abimelech."<sup>21</sup>And Jotham ran away and fled and went to Beer and lived there, because of Abimelech his brother.<sup>22</sup>Abimelech ruled over Israel three years.<sup>23</sup>And God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the leaders of Shechem, and the leaders of Shechem dealt treacherously with Abimelech,<sup>24</sup>that the violence done to the seventy sons of Jerubbaal might come, and their blood be laid on Abimelech their brother, who killed them, and on the men of Shechem, who strengthened his hands to kill his brothers.<sup>25</sup>And the leaders of Shechem put men in ambush against him on the mountaintops, and they robbed all who passed by them along that way. And it was told to Abimelech.<sup>26</sup>And Gaal the son of Ebed moved into Shechem with his relatives, and the leaders of Shechem put confidence in him.<sup>27</sup>And they went out into the field and gathered the grapes from their vineyards and trod them and held a festival; and they went into the house of their god and ate and drank and reviled Abimelech.<sup>28</sup>And Gaal the son of Ebed said, "Who is Abimelech, and who are we of Shechem, that we should serve him? Is he not the son of Jerubbaal, and is not Zebul his officer? Serve the men of Hamor the father of Shechem; but why should we serve him?<sup>29</sup>Would that this people were under my hand! Then I would remove Abimelech. I would say to Abimelech, 'Increase your army, and come out.'"<sup>30</sup>When Zebul the ruler of the city heard the words of Gaal the son of Ebed, his anger was kindled.<sup>31</sup>And he sent messengers to Abimelech secretly, saying, "Behold, Gaal the son of Ebed and his relatives have come to Shechem, and they are stirring up the city against you.<sup>32</sup>Now therefore, go by night, you and the people who are with you, and set an ambush in the field.<sup>33</sup>Then in the morning, as soon as the sun is up, rise early and rush upon the city. And when he and the people who are with him come out against you, you may do to them as your hand finds to do."<sup>34</sup>So Abimelech and all the men who were with him rose up by night and set an ambush against Shechem in four companies.<sup>35</sup>And Gaal the son of Ebed went out and stood in the entrance of the gate of the city, and Abimelech and the people who were with him rose from the ambush.<sup>36</sup>And when Gaal saw the people, he said to Zebul, "Look, people are coming down from the mountaintops!" And Zebul said to him, "You mistake the shadow of the mountains for men."<sup>37</sup>Gaal spoke again and said, "Look, people are coming down from the center of the land, and one company is coming from the direction of the Diviners' Oak."<sup>38</sup>Then Zebul said to him, "Where is your mouth now, you who said, 'Who is Abimelech, that we should serve him?' Are not these the people whom you despised? Go out now and fight with them."<sup>39</sup>And Gaal went out at the head of the leaders of Shechem and fought with Abimelech.<sup>40</sup>And Abimelech chased him, and he fled before him. And many fell wounded, up to the entrance of the gate.<sup>41</sup>And Abimelech lived at Arumah, and Zebul drove out Gaal and his relatives, so that they could not dwell at Shechem.<sup>42</sup>On the following day, the people went out into the field, and Abimelech was told.<sup>43</sup>He took his people and divided them into three companies and set an ambush in the fields. And he looked and saw the people coming out of the city. So he rose against them and killed them.<sup>44</sup>Abimelech and the company that was with him rushed forward and stood at the entrance of the gate of the city, while the two companies rushed upon all who were in the field and killed them.<sup>45</sup>And Abimelech fought against the city all that day. He captured the city and killed the people who were in it, and he razed the city and sowed it with salt.<sup>46</sup>When all the leaders of the Tower of Shechem heard of it, they entered the stronghold of the house of El-berith.<sup>47</sup>Abimelech was told that all the leaders of the Tower of Shechem were gathered together.<sup>48</sup>And Abimelech went up to Mount Zalmon, he and all the people who were with him. And Abimelech took an axe in his hand and cut down a bundle of brushwood and took it up and laid it on his shoulder. And he said to the men who were with him, "What you have seen me do, hurry and do as I have done."<sup>49</sup>So every one of the people cut down his bundle and following Abimelech put it against the stronghold, and they set the stronghold on fire over them, so that all the people of the Tower of Shechem also died, about 1,000 men and women.<sup>50</sup>Then Abimelech went to Thebez and encamped against Thebez and captured it.<sup>51</sup>But there was a strong tower within the city, and all the men and women and all the leaders of the city fled to it and shut themselves in, and they went up to the roof of the tower.<sup>52</sup>And Abimelech came to the tower and fought against it and drew near to the door of the tower to burn it with fire.<sup>53</sup>And a certain woman threw an upper millstone on Abimelech's head and crushed his skull.<sup>54</sup>Then he called quickly to the young man his armor-bearer and said to him, "Draw your sword and kill me, lest they say of me, 'A woman killed him.'" And his young man thrust him through, and he died.<sup>55</sup>And when the men of Israel saw that Abimelech was dead, everyone departed to his home.<sup>56</sup>Thus God returned the evil of Abimelech, which he committed against his father in killing his seventy brothers.<sup>57</sup>And God also made all the evil of the men of Shechem return on their heads, and upon them came the curse of Jotham the son of Jerubbaal.
9.overview:
Chapter 9 is the dark sequel to Gideon's golden ephod, the story of the anti-judge Abimelech. Where every other judge was raised up by God, Abimelech seizes power by murder. He is not sent; he grasps. He is not Spirit-clothed; he is ambition incarnate. If the judges are flawed types of Christ, Abimelech is a type of the antichrist — the self-appointed king who comes in his own name, builds his throne on blood, and brings ruin on all who follow him.

Abimelech persuades the men of Shechem to back his bid, hires reckless men with idol money, and murders his seventy brothers 'on one stone.' Only the youngest, Jotham, escapes. From Mount Gerizim Jotham shouts down the parable of the trees who sought a king: the fruitful olive, fig, and vine all decline the throne, and only the worthless, fire-prone bramble accepts — and its acceptance carries a threat of fire.

Jotham's curse comes true with terrible precision. God sends 'an evil spirit between Abimelech and the leaders of Shechem,' and they turn on each other. Abimelech destroys Shechem, sows it with salt, and burns a thousand people alive in its tower. Then, besieging Thebez, he is felled by a millstone dropped by a woman, and dies begging his armor-bearer to kill him lest it be said a woman slew him.

The narrator's verdict is stark: 'Thus God returned the evil of Abimelech.' Sin reaps what it sows; the fire of the bramble consumes the bramble (Gal. 6:7). The chapter is a thunderous demonstration that God governs even the schemes of wicked men, repaying blood with blood and vindicating the murdered seventy — and a dark backdrop against which the true King, who builds his kingdom not on his brothers' blood but on his own, shines all the brighter.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Abimelech Seizes Power by Murder
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Abimelech appeals to his Shechemite kinsmen, hires reckless men with temple silver, and murders his seventy brothers on one stone. Only Jotham escapes. Shechem crowns Abimelech king.
verseByVerse.theology: Abimelech is the anti-judge: not raised by God but self-appointed, building his throne on fratricide and idol money. He is the antithesis of the King who emptied himself for his brothers.
verseByVerse.examples: Ambition that grasps what God has not given builds on blood. The kingdom of self is founded on the destruction of rivals.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Abimelech the son of Jerubbaal went to Shechem to his mother's relatives and said to them... "Which is better for you, that all seventy of the sons of Jerubbaal rule over you, or that one rule over you? Remember also that I am your bone and your flesh." ...their hearts inclined to follow Abimelech...
verseByVerse.commentary: Abimelech opens his campaign with cynical manipulation. He appeals to his mother's kinsmen in Shechem on the basis of blood — 'I am your bone and your flesh' — and invents a threat that does not exist, suggesting the seventy sons of Gideon intend to rule them, when there is no evidence they sought any such thing. He offers himself as the convenient local alternative. Davis notes how Abimelech trades entirely on flesh and clan, never on calling or righteousness; he is the first man in the book to grasp at leadership rather than be raised to it by God. Every true judge was sent — Othniel raised up, Gideon called from the winepress, the Spirit clothing each one. Abimelech sends himself. The contrast is the heart of the chapter. He appeals to tribal self-interest ('better for you'), not to the glory of God or the good of Israel. This is the politics of the flesh, the campaign of ambition, and the Shechemites' hearts 'inclined to follow' him because he spoke to their pride and their pocketbooks. He stands in utter opposition to the King who would not grasp at glory but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Phil. 2:6–7). Abimelech reaches up to seize a throne; Christ reached down to wash feet. (cf. Phil. 2:6–7; John 5:43)

verseByVerse.quote: And they gave him seventy pieces of silver out of the house of Baal-berith with which Abimelech hired worthless and reckless fellows, who followed him. And he went to his father's house at Ophrah and killed his brothers the sons of Jerubbaal, seventy men, on one stone. But Jotham the youngest son of Jerubbaal was left, for he hid himself.
verseByVerse.commentary: The Shechemites finance Abimelech with seventy pieces of silver from the temple of Baal-berith — idol money for an idolatrous king — and with it he hires 'worthless and reckless fellows,' the violent hangers-on who attach themselves to any strongman. Then comes the atrocity: he goes to Ophrah and murders his seventy brothers 'on one stone.' The phrase is chilling in its efficiency — a butcher's block, an assembly-line slaughter of his own family to eliminate every rival to the throne. The number seventy echoes back to chapter 1, where the Canaanite tyrant Adoni-bezek had mutilated seventy kings; now an Israelite does far worse, murdering seventy of his own brothers. Davis observes that the line between Canaan and Israel has all but vanished — God's people now produce tyrants worse than the pagans they were sent to drive out. Only Jotham, the youngest, escapes by hiding, and the men of Shechem crown Abimelech king, ironically near the very place where Joshua had renewed the covenant (Josh. 24). The throne is built on fratricide and financed by idolatry. This is the kingdom of self, and its foundation stone is murder — the dark inverse of the King who builds his kingdom on his own blood shed for his brothers. (cf. Gen. 4:8; Heb. 2:11)

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–15 — Jotham's Parable of the Trees
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: From Mount Gerizim Jotham shouts the fable of the trees seeking a king: the olive, fig, and vine all refuse to abandon their fruitfulness, but the worthless bramble accepts — offering false shade and threatening fire.
verseByVerse.theology: The worthy decline the crown to keep bearing fruit; the worthless grasp it and bring fire, not shade. Human kingship apart from God produces a furnace, not a refuge.
verseByVerse.examples: Those most fit to lead are often least eager for power; those least fit grasp it most greedily. The bramble king gives no shade, only fire.

verseByVerse.quote: ...he cried out, "...The trees once went out to anoint a king over them, and they said to the olive tree, 'Reign over us.' But the olive tree said to them, 'Shall I leave my abundance... and go hold sway over the trees?'" ...the fig tree... the vine... [all refused].
verseByVerse.commentary: The lone survivor climbs Mount Gerizim — the mountain of blessing in Israel's covenant ceremony — and shouts down a fable of devastating wit. The trees once went out to anoint a king. They asked the olive tree, but it refused: 'Shall I leave my abundance, by which gods and men are honored, and go hold sway over the trees?' They asked the fig tree, which would not forsake its sweetness and good fruit; and the vine, which would not abandon its wine 'that cheers God and men.' The worthy trees — the fruitful, useful ones — all decline the throne. Davis draws out the searching truth: those most fit to lead are often least eager for power, precisely because they are busy bearing fruit. The olive, fig, and vine each have a calling they will not abandon for the empty 'swaying over the trees.' There is wisdom here about the right attitude toward power and position. The mature servant of God does not crave the crown; he is content to be fruitful in his appointed place, producing oil and sweetness and wine for the good of others rather than lording it over them. The craving for preeminence is itself a mark of the bramble. The fruitful are too useful to be ambitious. Jesus would say it directly: the one who would be great must be the servant of all (Mark 10:43–44). (cf. Mark 10:43–44; 3 John 9)

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the trees said to the bramble, "You come and reign over us." And the bramble said to the trees, "If in good faith you are anointing me king over you, then come and take refuge in my shade, but if not, let fire come out of the bramble and devour the cedars of Lebanon."
verseByVerse.commentary: At last the trees turn to the bramble — a worthless, fruitless, low-growing thornbush, good for nothing but kindling and a hazard in the dry season. And the bramble eagerly accepts, with a speech full of menace: 'If in good faith you are anointing me king over you, then come and take refuge in my shade, but if not, let fire come out of the bramble and devour the cedars of Lebanon.' The absurdity is the point. A thornbush offering shade is laughable, for it has none to give; one cannot shelter under a bramble. Its only real power is to catch fire and, in burning, set ablaze even the mighty cedars. Davis presses the searing truth: the worthless grasp for power most greedily, and the bramble king gives no shade, only fire. Abimelech is the bramble — fruitless, destructive, offering Israel a kingship that can shelter no one and will end in flames. The threat in the bramble's speech is the prophecy of the whole chapter: fire will come out and devour. This stands in stark, glorious contrast to the true King, the Vine of John 15, who did not cling to glory but came down to give his people shade and fruit and life, laying down his own life for the trees of his planting. Jotham's bramble is the antithesis of Christ, who is himself the refuge that does not burn. (cf. John 15:1; Isa. 32:2)

verseByVerse.quote: "Now therefore, if you acted in good faith and integrity when you made Abimelech king... then rejoice in Abimelech... But if not, let fire come out from Abimelech and devour the leaders of Shechem... and let fire come out from the leaders of Shechem... and devour Abimelech." And Jotham ran away and fled...
verseByVerse.commentary: Jotham makes the parable's application explicit and unsparing. If Shechem has dealt honestly with Gideon's house, let them rejoice in Abimelech. But if they have acted treacherously — and they have, financing the slaughter of Gideon's seventy sons — then he pronounces the double curse: 'let fire come out from Abimelech and devour the leaders of Shechem... and let fire come out from the leaders of Shechem... and devour Abimelech.' The bramble and those who crowned it will consume each other in flames. It is a curse that is really a prophecy, a sentence Jotham announces but God will execute. Davis notes that Jotham appeals to 'good faith and integrity' — the moral order that Abimelech and Shechem have shattered — and entrusts the verdict to God by fleeing rather than fighting. He does not take vengeance into his own hands; he speaks the truth and leaves the outcome to the God who judges. There is wisdom in this. The wronged believer is not called to execute justice personally but to declare what is right and commit the matter to the righteous Judge. Jotham flees to Beer and lives; the curse he pronounced will do its slow, certain work. The God who governs all things will see that fire comes out exactly as Jotham said, for he will not be mocked, and the seventy sons' blood will not go unanswered. (cf. Rom. 12:19; Ps. 7:15–16)

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–29 — The Evil Spirit and the Rebellion of Gaal
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After three years God sends an evil spirit between Abimelech and Shechem, that the murder of the seventy might be avenged. Gaal son of Ebed arrives and stirs Shechem to rebellion.
verseByVerse.theology: God sovereignly governs even the treachery of wicked men, turning their mutual hatred into the instrument of his justice. The blood of the seventy will be repaid.
verseByVerse.examples: God needs no new weapons to judge the wicked; he simply lets their sin run its course among themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: Abimelech ruled over Israel three years. And God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the leaders of Shechem... that the violence done to the seventy sons of Jerubbaal might come, and their blood be laid on Abimelech their brother, who killed them, and on the men of Shechem, who strengthened his hands to kill his brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary: Abimelech rules three years, and then the curse begins to work. The narrator states it with stark theological clarity: 'God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the leaders of Shechem.' Here is the sovereignty of God over even the wickedness of wicked men. The 'evil spirit' is best understood as a spirit of discord and ill will that God permits and directs; he does not author their sin, but he governs it, turning the murderers' mutual treachery into the instrument of his judgment. And the purpose is stated plainly: 'that the violence done to the seventy sons of Jerubbaal might come, and their blood be laid on Abimelech... and on the men of Shechem, who strengthened his hands.' Both the tyrant and his accomplices will be repaid. Davis underscores the bedrock truth: God's moral government is inescapable, and he often executes justice not by sending some new calamity but simply by letting sinners reap the sin they have sown among themselves. The murderers turn on each other; the conspirators devour one another. The blood of the innocent seventy cries from the ground, and God answers — not with a thunderbolt, but by setting the wicked against the wicked. He who shed innocent blood will have his own blood required. The God who governs the evil spirit between Abimelech and Shechem governs every scheme of every tyrant still. (cf. 1 Sam. 16:14; Gen. 4:10)

verseByVerse.quote: And Gaal the son of Ebed moved into Shechem with his relatives, and the leaders of Shechem put confidence in him. ...Gaal the son of Ebed said, "Who is Abimelech, and who are we of Shechem, that we should serve him?..."
verseByVerse.commentary: The instrument of discord arrives in the person of Gaal son of Ebed, a newcomer who wins the confidence of Shechem's leaders. At the vintage festival, amid the feasting and drinking in the house of their god, Gaal grows bold and drunkenly contemptuous of Abimelech: 'Who is Abimelech, and who are we of Shechem, that we should serve him?' He boasts that if the people were under his command, he would remove Abimelech. The very Shechemites who crowned Abimelech now itch to be rid of him, their loyalty as cheap and shifting as the silver they paid for murder. Davis notes the bitter logic of treachery: those who will betray for gain will betray again, and the man who gained a throne by violence cannot trust the violent men who gave it to him. There is no honor among the godless; the alliance of the wicked is a rope of sand. Gaal's drunken boast is the spark, but the fire was laid by God's evil spirit of discord, working out the curse. The whole sordid scene — the festival in the pagan temple, the drunken treason, the shifting loyalties — is a portrait of a society that has forgotten God and now feeds on itself. When men cast off the fear of the LORD, they do not become free; they become wolves to one another. Shechem's rebellion against the tyrant it created is the next turn of the wheel of judgment Jotham foretold. (cf. Prov. 26:24–26; Gal. 5:15)

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Warned by his officer Zebul, Abimelech ambushes Gaal and routs him, then captures Shechem, kills its people, sows the city with salt, and burns about a thousand people alive in the tower of Shechem.
verseByVerse.theology: Jotham's prophecy is fulfilled to the letter: fire comes out from Abimelech and devours the leaders of Shechem. Human kingship apart from God produces not refuge but a furnace.
verseByVerse.examples: The fire of ambition, once kindled, does not stay where it is lit; it spreads until it consumes both the kindler and all who warmed themselves at it.

verseByVerse.quote: When Zebul the ruler of the city heard the words of Gaal... his anger was kindled. And he sent messengers to Abimelech secretly... So Abimelech... fought with [Gaal]. And Gaal fled before him... Thus Zebul drove out Gaal and his relatives, so that they could not dwell at Shechem.
verseByVerse.commentary: Zebul, Abimelech's loyal officer within Shechem, secretly warns his master of Gaal's rebellion and counsels an ambush. Abimelech lies in wait, and when Gaal comes out at dawn, Zebul taunts him into battle. Gaal's drunken bravado collapses in the cold light of morning; he is routed and driven from the city, his rebellion crushed before it could rise. The treacherous are outmaneuvered by the more treacherous. Davis observes the grim spectacle of the wicked devouring one another — Zebul betraying Gaal to Abimelech, Abimelech preparing to destroy the very Shechem that made him king. There is no virtue in any party here; this is simply the curse working itself out, the evil spirit of discord doing its appointed labor. The reader feels the gathering momentum of judgment. Gaal, the would-be liberator, proves a drunken windbag who flees at the first clash; Zebul, the schemer, secures a temporary victory for a doomed master; and Abimelech, the bramble king, turns now in fury upon his own people. Every alliance among the godless is provisional, every loyalty for sale, every victory a prelude to the next betrayal. This is the kingdom of self at war with itself, and it can end only in ashes. The God who governs it is patiently bringing the blood of the seventy back upon the heads that shed it. (cf. Prov. 11:5; Ps. 9:15–16)

verseByVerse.quote: ...Abimelech captured the city and killed the people who were in it, and he razed the city and sowed it with salt. ...all the people of the Tower of Shechem... entered the stronghold of the house of El-berith. ...Abimelech... set the stronghold on fire over them, so that all the people of the Tower of Shechem also died, about 1,000 men and women.
verseByVerse.commentary: Abimelech's vengeance on the city that crowned him is total. He captures Shechem, slaughters its people, razes it to the ground, and sows it with salt — an act of permanent, symbolic destruction, declaring the soil forever cursed and barren. The king destroys the very city that made him king. Then the horror climaxes: about a thousand men and women take refuge in the stronghold of the temple of El-berith, the tower of Shechem. Abimelech and his men cut brushwood, pile it against the stronghold, and set it ablaze, and 'all the people of the Tower of Shechem also died, about a thousand men and women.' Jotham's prophecy is fulfilled to the letter: fire came out from Abimelech and devoured the leaders of Shechem. The bramble's fire, threatened in verse 15, has now consumed. Davis refuses to soften the scene, and neither should we: a thousand people burned alive in their false refuge is one of the most harrowing images in the book, a vision of what human kingship apart from God finally produces — not shade, but fire; not refuge, but a furnace. This is the bitter harvest of the golden ephod, the wages of seizing what God did not give, the end of a nation that does what is right in its own eyes. The fire of ambition, once kindled, does not stay where it is lit. Only the kingdom that comes down from heaven, founded on mercy not murder, offers a refuge that does not burn. (cf. Gal. 6:8; Ps. 11:6)

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 50–57 — The Millstone of Thebez and God's Retribution
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Besieging Thebez, Abimelech approaches the tower to burn it, but a woman drops a millstone that crushes his skull. He begs his armor-bearer to kill him lest it be said a woman slew him. The narrator declares: thus God returned the evil of Abimelech and the men of Shechem.
verseByVerse.theology: God topples the proud through the weak — a woman's millstone, echoing Jael's tent peg and the seed of the woman crushing the serpent. God returns evil on the head that devised it; a man reaps what he sows.
verseByVerse.examples: Vengeance belongs to God, who repays all innocent blood. For those who shelter in the true King, there is a blood that speaks not vengeance but forgiveness.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Abimelech went to Thebez and... there was a strong tower within the city, and all... fled to it... And Abimelech came to the tower and fought against it... And a certain woman threw an upper millstone on Abimelech's head and crushed his skull. Then he called quickly to the young man his armor-bearer and said... "Draw your sword and kill me, lest they say of me, 'A woman killed him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: Drunk on destruction, Abimelech marches against Thebez, but its people flee to a strong tower. As he approaches to burn it as he burned Shechem's, God's justice strikes with poetic precision: 'a certain woman threw an upper millstone on Abimelech's head and crushed his skull.' The mighty bramble king, who slaughtered seventy brothers and burned a thousand people, is felled by an anonymous woman with a household grinding-stone dropped from a tower. The reversal echoes Sisera, brought down by Jael's tent peg, and reaches back to Genesis 3:15 — the seed of the woman crushing the serpent's head. God delights to topple the proud through the weak and despised. Mortally wounded, Abimelech's last concern is not his soul but his reputation: 'kill me, lest they say of me, A woman killed him.' Even dying, vanity rules him; he fears the shame of a woman's blow more than death or judgment itself. So his armor-bearer runs him through. Davis notes the bitter futility — his attempt to hide the shame failed utterly, for the story was told and retold, remembered centuries later (2 Sam. 11:21). The man who built his throne on blood dies as a byword, undone by a woman and a millstone, clutching at his pride to the last breath. Pride goes before destruction; the proud heart is its own executioner. (cf. Gen. 3:15; Prov. 16:18)

verseByVerse.quote: Thus God returned the evil of Abimelech, which he committed against his father in killing his seventy brothers. And God also made all the evil of the men of Shechem return on their heads, and upon them came the curse of Jotham the son of Jerubbaal.
verseByVerse.commentary: The narrator delivers the chapter's theological verdict, and he says it twice for emphasis: 'Thus God returned the evil of Abimelech... And God also made all the evil of the men of Shechem return on their heads.' Note the agent of every clause — God returned, God made return. Behind the millstone, the civil war, the evil spirit, the whole bloody unraveling, stands the moral government of God, who will not be mocked and who repays. Jotham's curse was no empty rhetoric but the announcement of a sentence God himself executed. Davis underscores the bedrock truth that anchors the chapter: a man reaps what he sows (Gal. 6:7). Abimelech sowed his brothers' blood and reaped his own; the men of Shechem sowed treachery and reaped fire. The justice is exact, the harvest unavoidable. And in this dark vindication there is, for the believer, profound hope. The God who avenged the murdered seventy is the God who hears all innocent blood crying from the ground (Gen. 4:10), who will set every wrong right in his time, who reserves vengeance to himself so that we need not seize it (Rom. 12:19). The bramble king's fire consumed the bramble. But for those who shelter in the true King, there is a refuge that does not burn and a blood that does not cry for vengeance but speaks a better word — the sprinkled blood of Jesus, which pleads not 'condemn' but 'forgive.' (cf. Gal. 6:7; Heb. 12:24)

9.theology:
The Anti-Judge. Every true judge was raised up by God and clothed with his Spirit; Abimelech seizes power by murder and rules by terror. He is the photographic negative of a deliverer, a type of the antichrist who comes in his own name — the antithesis of the King who emptied himself and gave his life for his brothers.

The Bramble King. Jotham's parable exposes a timeless truth: the worthy decline the crown to keep bearing fruit, while the worthless grasp it and bring fire, not shade. Human kingship apart from God produces not refuge but a furnace, pointing by contrast to the true Vine who gives life to his own.

God Returns the Evil: A Man Reaps What He Sows. 'Thus God returned the evil of Abimelech' (v. 56). The evil spirit, the civil war, the millstone — all are the moral government of God repaying blood with blood. He will not be mocked; vengeance is his (Gal. 6:7; Rom. 12:19).
9.examples:
Then: Abimelech murdered seventy brothers to seize a crown God never gave, ruled by terror, burned a thousand people in Shechem's tower, and died with his skull crushed by a woman's millstone — God returning his evil on his own head exactly as Jotham's curse foretold.

Now: Beware the bramble's ambition — the grasping for power, position, or recognition that God has not given. The fire of selfish ambition never stays where it is lit; it consumes the one who kindles it. Take comfort that God still governs the schemes of the wicked and repays all innocent blood — and flee for refuge to the King whose blood speaks not vengeance but forgiveness.

10.title: Tola, Jair, and Renewed Apostasy
10.text: <sup>1</sup>After Abimelech there arose to save Israel Tola the son of Puah, son of Dodo, a man of Issachar, and he lived at Shamir in the hill country of Ephraim.<sup>2</sup>And he judged Israel twenty-three years. Then he died and was buried at Shamir.<sup>3</sup>After him arose Jair the Gileadite, who judged Israel twenty-two years.<sup>4</sup>And he had thirty sons who rode on thirty donkeys, and they had thirty cities, called Havvoth-jair to this day, which are in the land of Gilead.<sup>5</sup>And Jair died and was buried in Kamon.<sup>6</sup>The people of Israel again did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and served the Baals and the Ashtaroth, the gods of Syria, the gods of Sidon, the gods of Moab, the gods of the Ammonites, and the gods of the Philistines. And they forsook the LORD and did not serve him.<sup>7</sup>So the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he sold them into the hand of the Philistines and into the hand of the Ammonites,<sup>8</sup>and they crushed and oppressed the people of Israel that year. For eighteen years they oppressed all the people of Israel who were beyond the Jordan in the land of the Amorites, which is in Gilead.<sup>9</sup>And the Ammonites crossed the Jordan to fight also against Judah and against Benjamin and against the house of Ephraim, so that Israel was severely distressed.<sup>10</sup>And the people of Israel cried out to the LORD, saying, "We have sinned against you, because we have forsaken our God and have served the Baals."<sup>11</sup>And the LORD said to the people of Israel, "Did I not save you from the Egyptians and from the Amorites, from the Ammonites and from the Philistines?<sup>12</sup>The Sidonians also, and the Amalekites and the Maonites oppressed you, and you cried out to me, and I saved you out of their hand.<sup>13</sup>Yet you have forsaken me and served other gods; therefore I will save you no more.<sup>14</sup>Go and cry out to the gods whom you have chosen; let them save you in the time of your distress."<sup>15</sup>And the people of Israel said to the LORD, "We have sinned; do to us whatever seems good to you. Only please deliver us this day."<sup>16</sup>So they put away the foreign gods from among them and served the LORD, and he became impatient over the misery of Israel.<sup>17</sup>Then the Ammonites were called to arms, and they encamped in Gilead. And the people of Israel came together, and they encamped at Mizpah.<sup>18</sup>And the people, the leaders of Gilead, said one to another, "Who is the man who will begin to fight against the Ammonites? He shall be head over all the inhabitants of Gilead."
10.overview:
Chapter 10 sits as a hinge in the book. It opens with two of the so-called 'minor judges,' Tola and Jair, briefly noted — men who 'judged Israel' but of whom no deliverance is recorded, only years and burial places. Then the chapter pivots into one of the most theologically searching exchanges in all of Judges: a divine dialogue in which God, exasperated by Israel's relentless idolatry, declares he will save them no more — and then, against his own announced verdict, cannot bear their misery.

Israel's apostasy here reaches a new breadth. They serve not just the Baals and Ashtaroth but the gods of Syria, Sidon, Moab, Ammon, and Philistia — a whole pantheon of foreign deities. The narrator says they 'forsook the LORD and did not serve him.' God's anger is kindled, and he sells them into the hands of the Philistines and the Ammonites, who crush and oppress them for eighteen years.

When Israel cries out, God's response is unlike anything earlier in the book. Instead of immediately raising a deliverer, he confronts them: 'Did I not save you from the Egyptians, the Amorites, the Ammonites, the Philistines...? Yet you have forsaken me. Therefore I will save you no more. Go and cry out to the gods whom you have chosen; let them save you.' It is the language of a wounded husband, a holy sarcasm that exposes the folly of idolatry — let the gods you preferred rescue you now.

And here the chapter reaches its astonishing climax. Israel does the one thing that moves the heart of God: they confess their sin, put away their foreign gods, and serve the LORD. And then comes the most tender line — 'he became impatient over the misery of Israel,' or as older versions render it, 'his soul was grieved for the misery of Israel.' The God who said 'I will save you no more' cannot, in the end, abandon his people. Here the gospel blazes: the LORD's love is not finally conditioned on Israel's worthiness but rooted in his own covenant heart. He is grieved by their pain even when it is self-inflicted. This is the God who would one day be so moved by our misery that he gave his only Son — the God whose mercy triumphs over the judgment his justice demands.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Tola and Jair, the Minor Judges
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Tola judges Israel twenty-three years; Jair judges twenty-two years, noted for his thirty sons on thirty donkeys with thirty towns. No deliverance is recorded — only quiet years and burial.
verseByVerse.theology: God provides ordinary, unspectacular leadership as well as dramatic deliverers. Faithfulness in obscurity has its own worth in God's economy.
verseByVerse.examples: Not every servant of God is a Gideon or a Samson. Quiet, faithful stewardship matters, even when no great deeds are recorded.

verseByVerse.quote: After Abimelech there arose to save Israel Tola the son of Puah... and he judged Israel twenty-three years. Then he died... After him arose Jair the Gileadite, who judged Israel twenty-two years. And he had thirty sons who rode on thirty donkeys, and they had thirty cities...
verseByVerse.commentary: After the nightmare of Abimelech, the narrator offers a moment of quiet with two 'minor' judges. Tola 'arose to save Israel' and judged twenty-three years; Jair the Gileadite judged twenty-two, notable mainly for his thirty sons riding thirty donkeys and holding thirty towns — a mark of prosperity and influence. Of neither man is any battle or deliverance recorded; we are told their years, their families, and their graves. They are easy to skim past, and that is part of their lesson. Davis notes that after the spectacular violence of Abimelech, these understated notices come almost as relief — forty-five combined years of stable, unremarkable leadership, the long stretches of ordinary faithfulness that hold a society together between crises. Not every servant of God is a Gideon routing Midian or a Samson toppling temples. Most of God's work in the world is done by Tolas and Jairs — faithful people whose names appear once, whose deeds fill no dramatic chapter, who simply judged Israel and died. There is dignity in such obscurity. The kingdom advances not only through the famous few but through the faithful many whose quiet stewardship leaves little record but real fruit. God sees the unspectacular servant; the cup of cold water given in his name is not forgotten (Matt. 10:42). Tola 'arose to save Israel,' and that is enough for the LORD to have recorded his name forever. (cf. Matt. 10:42; 1 Cor. 4:2)

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel's idolatry reaches new breadth — serving the gods of seven nations and forsaking the LORD entirely. God sells them to the Philistines and Ammonites, who crush them for eighteen years.
verseByVerse.theology: Apostasy deepens with each turn of the cycle. Israel now serves a whole pantheon of foreign gods, abandoning the LORD altogether — and the oppression intensifies accordingly.
verseByVerse.examples: Idolatry is rarely content with one idol; the heart that leaves God collects substitutes. The further we drift, the heavier the bondage.

verseByVerse.quote: The people of Israel again did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and served the Baals and the Ashtaroth, the gods of Syria, the gods of Sidon, the gods of Moab, the gods of the Ammonites, and the gods of the Philistines. And they forsook the LORD and did not serve him. So the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel...
verseByVerse.commentary: The cycle turns yet again — 'the people of Israel again did what was evil' — but now the apostasy reaches a staggering new breadth. Where earlier they served 'the Baals,' here they serve the gods of seven nations: Syria, Sidon, Moab, Ammon, Philistia, plus the Baals and Ashtaroth. They have assembled a whole pantheon, a veritable collector's cabinet of idols. And the summary verdict is total: 'they forsook the LORD and did not serve him.' Not partly, not occasionally — they abandoned him entirely. Davis observes the deepening of the spiral; each relapse in the book sinks lower than the last, and here Israel's idolatry becomes comprehensive, embracing every god but the true one. There is a spiritual law exposed here: idolatry is never satisfied with a single idol. The heart that forsakes the living God does not find one substitute and rest; it collects them, serving Sidon's gods on one day and Ammon's the next, ever restless, ever seeking, never filled. Augustine's words apply: the heart is restless until it rests in God, and so the apostate heart multiplies its idols in a hunger nothing false can satisfy. The consequence follows as surely as ever: God's anger is kindled, and the oppression that comes — Philistines and Ammonites crushing Israel for eighteen years — is heavier than before. The further the drift, the deeper the bondage. (cf. Jer. 2:13; Rom. 1:23)

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel cries out and confesses sin, but God responds with a stinging rehearsal of his past deliverances and a refusal: 'I will save you no more. Go and cry out to the gods whom you have chosen; let them save you.'
verseByVerse.theology: God's holy sarcasm exposes the folly of idolatry. The refusal is real but not final — it is meant to break Israel's shallow repentance into genuine turning.
